sides.position: Śaṅkara and Sureśvara: knowledge alone liberates; works purify the mind beforehand but cannot be combined with knowledge, whose object is the actionless self.
arguments: knowledge and action are opposed like light and darkness

sides.position: Gauḍīya: neither works nor knowledge but pure devotion is the means; works and the pursuit of impersonal knowledge 'cover' devotion (BRS 1.1.11); prescribed duties may be abandoned by one devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
arguments: BhP 10.14.3: those who give up effort for knowledge conquer him by hearing

reconciliation.explanation: The Rāma Gītā itself assigns action to the stage before knowledge (purification) and renunciation to the stage of knowledge.
reconciliation.detail: Read by stage (P4) both sides agree that action has a place; they still disagree whether it remains necessary after knowledge, which is not reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaita denies samuccaya at the stage of knowledge; Bhāskara's school holds combination to the end.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: works belong to the beginner's stage (mind purification), knowledge to the qualified (Śaṅkara's own framework).
P3-path: works and knowledge as paths for different temperaments (Īśa 1–2 as read by Śaṅkara).
Bhāmatī–Vivaraṇa difference (desire vs knowledge) as a difference of emphasis within the preparatory stage.
sequential (action then knowledge)
simultaneous combination (Bhāskara)
notes: A sub-debate of dsp:works-knowledge-grace (owned by U50); both sides are stated within the Rāma Gītā itself.

historical_debates.name: The debate of Śaṅkara and Maṇḍana Miśra at Māhiṣmatī
historical_debates.accounts: Śaṅkaradigvijaya cantos 8–10 (the tradition's account): judged by Ubhaya Bhāratī; Maṇḍana defeated and became Sureśvara.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita: Śaṅkara victorious; scholarly: the event is not historically attested and the identity of Maṇḍana and Sureśvara is doubted.

question: Is liberation reached by the yogī's body-discipline, or by the Name and the inner guru that the Sants set above it?

sides.position: The yogī reaches the supreme through the guru, restraint, bindu, the unstruck sound and sahaja; the Nāths themselves reject outward marks and sectarian worship ('neither temple nor mosque').
arguments: Gorakh Bānī sayings on restraint, the guru and the supreme state.

sides.position: Earrings, ash, matted hair and bodily yoga do not bring one to Rām; only love of the Name and the true guru's word do. In the Kabīr–Gorakh Goṣṭhī Kabīr is shown overcoming Gorakh.
arguments: Kabīr's sayings against the yogī's garb and practices (Bījak).
Kabīr–Gorakh Goṣṭhī.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled; the Kabīr side is to be stated from the Bījak by the owning unit (U27)
candidate_readings: P3-path: body-breath (Nāth) and devotion to the Name (Sant) as paths for different temperaments; both reject outward marks.
Shared vocabulary (sahaj, śūnya, anahad) suggests a common goal named from two paths.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth presents Gorakh as defeated, and Nāth sources do not accept Kabīr's authority; neither would accept being placed as an equal path.

historical_debates.name: Kabīr and Gorakh
historical_debates.accounts: Kabīr–Gorakh Goṣṭhī (a Kabīr Panth text).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: In the Kabīr Panth account Kabīr prevails.

question: Was Kabīr a disciple of Rāmānanda?

sides.position: Yes: Kabīr was one of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples; lying on the steps of the Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ he received the Name 'Rām' when Rāmānanda stepped on him; his Rām is Rāmānanda's.
arguments: the Rāmānandī hagiographies (Anantadās, Nābhādās) say so
the popular line 'kāśī meṃ ham pragaṭ bhae, rāmānand ceṭāe' (late, of doubtful authenticity)

sides.position: No human guru was needed: Kabīr is the Sat Puruṣ incarnate who came in every age; he accepted Rāmānanda outwardly only to establish the custom of taking a guru (some panth accounts even make Rāmānanda his disciple).
arguments: Kabīr appeared on a lotus and was not born of a womb
the Satguru of Kabīr's songs is the Lord, not a man

historical_debates.name: Hagiographical claims
historical_debates.accounts: Anantadās's Kabīr Paracaī and Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl vs the Kabīr Panth literature
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: each tradition maintains its account

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a question of lineage fact on which the two traditions' accounts differ.
candidate_readings: P6-upaya: the Kabīr Panth's own reading — Kabīr modelled discipleship as a skilful means; rejected by Rāmānandīs, who hold the discipleship real
P2-standpoint: outward initiation by Rāmānanda (social standpoint) and the inner satguru (the Lord) are both affirmed; rejected by the Kabīr Panth insofar as it makes Kabīr a disciple
Scholarly chronology (metadata only): Rāmānanda's traditional dates (c. 1299–1410) make direct discipleship difficult for a Kabīr of c. 1440–1518
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth rejects any account that subordinates Kabīr; the Rāmānandīs reject the claim that Kabīr needed no guru.

question: Was Kabīr a Hindu or a Muslim?

sides.position: A Vaiṣṇava devotee of Rām and disciple of Rāmānanda.

Neither: the Sat Puruṣ appeared as a child on a lotus at Lahartārā and was raised by the Muslim weavers Nīrū and Nīmā; at his death only flowers were found, divided for a samādhi and a tomb at Maghar.
Kabīr's own verses disown both: Hindu and Turk fight over Rām and Rahīm and neither knows the secret.

historical_debates.name: The dispute over Kabīr's body at Maghar
historical_debates.accounts: Kabīr Panth and popular hagiography; Maghar has both a samādhi and a mazār
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: flowers divided; both shrines stand

reconciliation.explanation: Under P2, 'Muslim weaver' (by upbringing), 'devotee of Rām' (by devotion) and 'neither' (by his own teaching) are statements from different standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Claims only that the accounts answer different questions; it does not settle the hagiographic facts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth rejects a human birth; the Rāmānandīs reject 'neither'; Muslim claims (e.g. Kabīr as a Sufi pīr) are outside this ontology's scope and recorded only as context.

question: Is the Rām of the Sants the avatāra, Rāma son of Daśaratha?

sides.position: No: 'the son of Daśaratha is praised in the three worlds, but the secret of Rām's name is other'; Rām is the unborn Lord in every body.
arguments: Rām pervades every body (musk in the deer)
what is born and dies is not the Lord

sides.position: The avatāras come from the regions of Kāl to keep order; the Saints come from the highest region; the Saints are above the avatāras.
arguments: the avatāras do not take souls beyond the three worlds

sides.position: Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are Kāl's sons; Kabīr, not the avatāras, frees souls.
Yes: the one whom the Vedas sing and sages meditate on is the son of Daśaratha, lord of Kosala, for the sake of his devotees; there is no difference between saguṇa and nirguṇa.
arguments: the formless takes form out of love for devotees

reconciliation.explanation: Under P3-path the same Rām is approached through the Name within (Sants) and through the avatāra's form (Rāmānandīs); Tulsīdās's own 'no difference between saguṇa and nirguṇa' supports this from the saguṇa side.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation claims only that both paths address one Lord; it does not claim the Sants accept the avatāra as supreme.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat reject equality: for them the avatāras belong to Kāl's domain. The Rāmānandīs reject any view that makes Rāma less than the supreme Brahman.

notes: A special case of dsp:saguna-nirguna (owned by U50).

question: Is the Kāpālika way (skull vow, insignia, liquor, consort, Bhairava rites) a path to liberation?

sides.position: As reported: knowing and wearing the insignia, meditation on the self in the yoni, and the Lord's own path of liquor and the beloved lead to release (voiced only through opponents and satirists).
arguments: Āgamaprāmāṇya (report); Mattavilāsa v. 7 (satire); Prabodhacandrodaya act 3 (hostile).

sides.position: Release comes only from knowing Brahman (Vāsudeva); these practices are outside the Veda.
arguments: Yāmuna: 'tam eva viditvā atimṛtyum eti...'.

sides.position: The Kāpālikas are deluded opponents defeated by Śaṅkara (hagiography) and by Viveka (allegorical drama).
arguments: Śaṅkaradigvijaya cantos 11, 15; Prabodhacandrodaya act 3.

historical_debates.name: Śaṅkara and the Kāpālikas (Ugrabhairava at Śrīśaila; Krakaca at Ujjayinī)
historical_debates.accounts: Mādhavīya Śaṅkaradigvijaya (opponent's hagiography)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita hagiography: the Kāpālikas are defeated; no Kāpālika account survives.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled - and not fairly reconcilable while the Kāpālika side survives only in opponents' words.
candidate_readings: Await any first-hand Kāpālika/Somasiddhānta text before assessing.
P6-upaya: the skull vow as penance modelled on the Lord's own act (Kūrma P. 2.31) - a reading the critics do not accept.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The critics deny any validity; no Kāpālika voice is available.

question: Must the body be perfected and made deathless (kāya-citti, kaṟpam) for liberation, or is knowledge alone enough, the body being a pot to be seen through?

sides.position: The body must be perfected: when it perishes the life perishes and firm true knowledge cannot be reached; nourishing the body nourishes the life (TM 724); kāya-citti removes karma (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14); vāci and kaṟpam give a lasting body (TM 722, 727).
arguments: Without a lasting body there is no time to reach knowledge (TM 724).
The Lord has made the body his temple (TM 725).

sides.position: Knowledge and grace alone: for the knower who has seen the true thing, what need of kaṟpam or yoga? (Kuṭampai 2, 22); stilling the mind is higher than every power (Tāyumāṉavar); the only medicine against death is never forgetting the Lord's feet (Paṭṭiṉattār); the body is a leaking pot to be left (Aḻukaṇṇi 8).
arguments: The means are not the goal (Kuṭampai).
Powers do not still the mind (Tāyumāṉavar).

reconciliation.explanation: P4-stage: body-perfection is a means for the seeker (TM 724 names it as the condition for reaching knowledge); Kuṭampai speaks to the one who has already reached it.
reconciliation.detail: TM 724 itself frames the body's care instrumentally ('firm true knowledge cannot be reached'); Kuṭampai's couplets are addressed to the realized (meyññāṉi).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Siddhars who seek the deathless body as the goal itself (the alchemical stream, Bogar) would not accept that it is only a means; Paṭṭiṉattār's contempt for the body is not merely a higher-stage view.

question: Can valid cognition, the means of knowledge and the categories be coherently defined (and so difference established)?

sides.position: Śrīharṣa: every proposed definition fails; the Advaitin can argue on the basis of commonly accepted usage without committing to the reality of the categories; only self-luminous consciousness is beyond refutation.
Nyāya (and later Navya-Nyāya, esp. Gaṅgeśa): definitions can be refined to meet the objections; the categories and difference are real and knowable.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a dialectical contest over the definability of knowledge.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Nyāya's definitions hold for empirical usage (which Śrīharṣa also allows), not as ultimate truths.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya denies that empirical validity is merely provisional.

question: What appears in erroneous cognition? (theories of error)

sides.position: The existent-and-non-existent (sadasatkhyāti): the erroneous object is sublated as there and not sublated as real elsewhere.
arguments: Error is not the appearance of the non-existent, nor of the existent, nor of the indescribable, nor appearance-as-other (SS 5.52–55); it is sadasatkhyāti (5.56).

sides.position: The indescribable (anirvacanīyakhyāti): the erroneous object is neither real nor unreal.
arguments: The Sāṃkhya Sūtra rejects this view (5.54); Advaita's own texts to be cited by U13.

sides.position: Appearance-as-other (anyathākhyāti): a real thing elsewhere appears as something it is not.
arguments: The Sāṃkhya Sūtra rejects this view (5.55); Nyāya's own texts to be cited by U11.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: each theory describes error from a different ontological standpoint (realist, indeterminist, relocation).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school rejects the others' accounts (SS 5.52–55).

question: Is Kṛṣṇa a form of Kālī, or is the Goddess a power of Kṛṣṇa?

sides.position: (Toḍala) The ten Mahāvidyās are the ten avatāras; 'Bhagavatī Kālī herself arose as the form of Kṛṣṇa' (10.11); Kālī is the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.42-43; Karpūrādistotra 12).

(Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava) Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself ('kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam', Bhāgavata 1.3.28); Durgā is his one power of creation, maintenance and dissolution, sustaining the worlds like his shadow and acting by his will (Brahmasaṃhitā 5.44).

reconciliation.explanation: Each tradition describes the relation of Goddess and Kṛṣṇa from the standpoint of its chosen deity (iṣṭa-devatā); both agree the two are inseparable as power and power-holder.
reconciliation.detail: Jīva Gosvāmin's commentary on the Brahmasaṃhitā itself cites 'yaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ saiva durgā' and speaks of the non-difference of power and powerful; the Toḍala makes Kṛṣṇa Kālī's form. The reconciliation records complementary standpoints only.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gauḍīya tradition rejects any subordination of Kṛṣṇa to the Goddess; the Śākta texts reject the Goddess's subordination to Kṛṣṇa. Both reject the claim that the two views are simply the same.

question: Is Kaula practice — the Kula worship with the five tattvas, the circle and the cremation ground — a legitimate path to liberation, or a departure from dharma?

sides.position: The Kaula path is the highest (Kulārṇava 2.7-8), both enjoyment and yoga (2.23-24), Vedic in essence (2.85), misunderstood by the deluded as musk is taken for mud (2.109); the realized Kaula is beyond injunction and prohibition (9.55-58). But it is harder than a sword's edge (2.122), must be given only to the tested (2.36; 14.9-14), and is condemned when practised for pleasure: wine alone gives no perfection (2.117), the wilful and uninitiated go to hell (5.96-105), and abandoning ritual out of false learning is heresy (9.130).

(Rudrayāmala, voiced by Vasiṣṭha) The Siddhas of Mahācīna drink, eat meat and live with women 'outside the Veda' — how can perfection come without Vedic rites? The text answers through the Buddha that the Kula path begins in purity and the paśu disposition and is Vedic in its own way; the question is the orthodox objection it sets out to meet.

(Samaya Śrīvidyā) The sixty-four (Kaula) tantras beguile the world, aim at powers and are outside the Veda; the three higher classes should follow only the Vedic Samaya way (Lakṣmīdhara on Saundaryalaharī 31).
(Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age the Kaula (vīra) disposition does not exist; worship must be pure and meatless (4.2-3).

historical_debates.name: The Vasiṣṭha–Buddha dialogue in Mahācīna (Rudrayāmala 17)
historical_debates.accounts: A narrative debate inside the text, not a recorded historical event.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vasiṣṭha accepts the Kula way and becomes a Siddha.

reconciliation.explanation: The Kaula texts address different eligibilities (P4) and speak of freedom from injunction only for the realized, from the ultimate standpoint (P1), while binding everyone else by the samayas and warnings.
reconciliation.detail: Kulārṇava 9.55-58 ('no injunction, no prohibition') is spoken of the Kaula who has reached the goal; 5.96-105 and 9.130 bind the practitioner. This reconciles the Kaula texts with their own warnings; it does not reconcile Kaula with the Samaya and orthodox Vedic rejection of the tattvas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Samaya Śrīvidyā and orthodox Vedic authorities reject the Kaula rites as such, not merely their misuse; the Kaula texts reject the claim that their way is non-Vedic.

notes: Related: dsp:authority-of-sixty-four-tantras (U08), dsp:purity-impurity-kaula (U19), dsp:daksina-vs-vama.

question: At liberation, are the Lord's qualities transferred to, possessed by or produced in the soul - or is the soul's own Śiva-nature manifested?

sides.position: The liberated gains the Lord's qualities: powers of knowing and acting, the marks of perfection, union with Rudra ('attainment of the qualities' as the gain of the fifth stage).
arguments: PS 1.21-38; PABh on PS 5.29 ('guṇāvāpti'); SDS ch. 6.

sides.position: Liberation is the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature, not the transfer, possession or production of qualities; it comes through initiation, the Lord's act.
arguments: Rāmakaṇṭha, Kiraṇavṛtti ch. 1.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Siddhānta explicitly rejects accounts in which the Lord's qualities come to the soul from outside.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: described from the Lord's giving (Pāśupata) or from the soul's latent nature (Siddhānta).
No reconciliation: the Siddhānta's rejection is explicit.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Rāmakaṇṭha denies saṅkrānti, āveśa and samutpatti by name; which rival schools held them is not stated in the passage.

question: Does the liberated soul become identical with Śiva, or only equal to Śiva (śivasamatva) while remaining distinct?

sides.position: Sanskrit exegetes: the freed soul becomes a Śiva, equal in omniscience and omnipotence, its own powers manifested; it remains distinct and does not perform the cosmic acts; the liberations of other schools (isolation, extinction, merger) are refuted.

Tamil school: release is inseparable union (advaita as ananya) — the soul, its malas powerless, abides in Śiva enjoying his bliss, 'one, other and together'; it neither becomes Śiva nor stands as a second Lord; 'Śivasamavāda' and 'Saṅkrāntavāda' are refuted.
The liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva in omniscience and omnipotence but remains numerically distinct; the five cosmic acts remain Śiva's alone.

There is only one Maheśvara, the self of all beings (ĪPK 4.1); the bound individual already performs the five acts (PH 10); liberation is the recognition of that identity, culminating in lordship over the circle of one's own powers (PH 20). The Śiva Sūtra's 'he becomes like Śiva' (3.25) is read by Kṣemarāja in this sense.

reconciliation.explanation: Within the Siddhānta the two sides may be complementary standpoints (analytic: the soul's manifest powers; experiential: its enjoyment in Śiva); not yet reconciled with the non-dualists.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tamil authors reject 'equality' readings that make the soul a second agent; Sanskrit exegetes reject any merger that ends the soul's distinctness; both reject identity.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: 'equality' from the standpoint of plurality of knowers, 'identity' from the standpoint of the one consciousness.
Treat as a case of dsp:souls-one-or-distinct (U50) and reconcile there.
P2-standpoint between Sanskrit and Tamil Siddhānta
queued against Pratyabhijñā and Advaita identity
notes: U18 contributes the Sanskrit-exegete and Tamil-school sides to U19's dispute.
alt_notes: Siddhānta side from general knowledge; verse anchors to be supplied by U18.

question: Is the Liṅgāyata/Vīraśaiva tradition a religion distinct from 'Hinduism' and the Vedic fold, or a Śaiva sampradāya within it — and are 'Liṅgāyata' and 'Vīraśaiva' one tradition or two?

sides.position: Liṅgāyata is a distinct religion founded by Basava; it rejects the Veda, caste, temple worship and brāhmaṇical ritual; 'Vīraśaiva' names a Vedic-Āgamic Śaiva sect that is not the same as Basava's Liṅgāyata (the position of many Basava-centred writers and some Virakta maṭhas).
arguments: Basava puts the Veda to the touchstone and the vacanas reject caste and sacrifice.
The vacanas, not Veda or Āgama, are the scripture.

sides.position: Vīraśaiva and Liṅgāyata are two names of one tradition, which has its own identity and scriptures (a position taken by many who reject the split of the names, whether or not they regard the tradition as outside Hinduism).
arguments: Both strands wear the iṣṭaliṅga, follow the ṣaṭsthala and honour Basava.

sides.position: Vīraśaivism is a Śaiva sampradāya within Sanātana dharma, agreeing with the Veda and Vedānta, whose scripture includes the Āgamas, the SSM and the Śrīkarabhāṣya (the Pañcācārya position as generally stated).
arguments: The SSM declares the Śaiva Siddhānta Veda-consonant and its doctrine agreeing with Veda and Vedānta.
Early-20th-c. Sanskrit prints present Vīraśaiva dharma as that of 'liṅga-bearing brāhmaṇas'.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled; recorded as the tradition's internal debate without taking sides
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the question is answered differently from a doctrinal standpoint (relation to Veda) and a communal one (distinct institutions and rites).
The names track the two strands (śaraṇa and Pañcācārya) rather than two religions.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advocates of each position reject its reduction to a matter of standpoint.

historical_debates.name: Campaign for recognition of Liṅgāyata as a separate religion
historical_debates.accounts: In 2017–18 a public movement sought legal recognition of the Liṅgāyata (or Vīraśaiva-Liṅgāyata) community as a separate religion; the Government of Karnataka recommended minority-religion status in 2018 and the central government did not grant it (moderate confidence on details).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Disagreement persisted between the positions recorded above.

notes: Modern debate recorded only as the tradition's internal dispute; no side is endorsed.

question: Where does ignorance (avidyā) reside — in the individual self (jīva) or in Brahman?

sides.position: Ignorance resides in the individual selves, with Brahman as its object; there are as many ignorances as jīvas.
arguments: Pure Brahman, being knowledge itself, cannot be ignorant.
The jīva and ignorance presuppose each other beginninglessly like seed and sprout, so there is no vicious circle.
Liberation of one does not liberate all, which many ignorances explain.

sides.position: Pure consciousness (Brahman) is both the locus and the object of the one ignorance.
arguments: Only consciousness can be the locus of ignorance; the insentient cannot be ignorant.
The jīva is itself a product of ignorance and so cannot be its locus without circularity.
Experience 'I do not know Brahman' shows ignorance veiling consciousness itself.

reconciliation.explanation: The tradition itself treats both as empirical-level explanatory methods (prakriyā) converging on the one self; at the ultimate level there is no ignorance to locate.
reconciliation.detail: Grounded in Sureśvara's principle that any method leading to knowledge of the inner self is valid (BĀU-Vārttika 1.4.402) and Appayya's statement that the ancients, intent on the oneness of the self, were indifferent to how the empirical is explained (SLS opening). GK 2.32 and the Advaita view that avidyā is indescribable make the question one about the empirical explanation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Partisans on each side (Amalānanda for the Bhāmatī; Prakāśātman, Madhusūdana for the Vivaraṇa) argue that the other view is untenable, not merely another method; the reconciliation holds only at the level of the ultimate purport, not of the theories.

question: Should the liberated renouncer act for the world's good — teach, take disciples, follow scriptural conduct?

sides.position: No: he undertakes nothing for the world's welfare, takes no disciples, keeps no books, gives no lectures; gathering disciples binds.
arguments: Nāradaparivrājaka 5.19–22
Sannyāsa 2.79–85

sides.position: Yes, freely: though his work is done, he may keep to the scriptural path out of a wish to help the world — it does him no harm.
arguments: Avadhūta 23

reconciliation.explanation: The prohibitions bind the renouncer on the way; the Avadhūta speaks of the one whose work is done, and the Sannyāsa's rule itself exempts disciples taken out of compassion.
reconciliation.detail: Sannyāsa 2.79–85 names gathering disciples for service, gain, worship or fame — not out of compassion — as binding.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Nāradaparivrājaka states the prohibition without such an exception.

notes: Compare the Bhagavad Gītā's teaching on acting for the world's welfare (src:bhagavad-gita 3.20–25).

question: Can the Lord be only the efficient cause of the world, as the Māheśvaras teach? (Brahma Sūtra 2.2.37ff, paśupati-adhikaraṇa)

sides.position: The Lord is the cause; the effect - vidyā, kalā, paśu - is eternal and depends on him; Rudra is the efficient cause, his Kalā the other cause (as Yāmuna reports).
arguments: The Lord produces, favours and conceals the effect in play (PABh on PS 1.9).
As a potter is only the efficient cause of a pot, a conscious ruler is only the efficient cause (their reasoning as reported by Vācaspati).

sides.position: Brahman is both the material and the efficient cause; the view of a Lord who is only ruler is non-Vedic and inconsistent (partiality, no possible relation, no support for ruling insentient matter, finitude or non-omniscience).
arguments: Patyur asāmañjasyāt (BS 2.2.37) and the following sūtras, as explained by Śaṅkara.

sides.position: The Paśupati doctrine is contrary to the Veda and internally inconsistent; its practices (insignia, skull-eating, corpse-ash) are non-Vedic.
arguments: Rāmānuja on the paśupati-adhikaraṇa, following Yāmuna.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the disagreement concerns whether the Lord is also the material cause of the world.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pāśupata analyses the world as eternal effect under a ruler (causal standpoint); Vedānta speaks of Brahman as the substance of all (substance standpoint).
No reconciliation: Vedānta treats the non-material-cause view as contrary to śruti.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both Vedānta schools reject the Pāśupata view as non-Vedic; the Pāśupatas count Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya causes among the effects (PABh 5.46).

question: Are the scriptural passages Madhva quotes from works not otherwise known (e.g. 'Bhāllaveya śruti', 'Brahmatarka', 'Paramaśruti') authentic scripture?

sides.position: They are genuine scripture — quoted from Vedic recensions, Pañcarātra texts and Purāṇa portions available to Madhva but now rare or lost; Madhva, as Vāyu's avatāra who received the Vedas' meaning from Vyāsa, had access to them.
arguments: many old texts have been lost
Madhva's authority as Vāyu's avatāra and Vyāsa's disciple

sides.position: Critics of Madhva have questioned the authority of quotations that cannot be traced in known texts and declined to accept them as scripture.
arguments: the passages are not found in the known recensions

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled — a question of textual history, outside the reconciliation principles.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Dvaita tradition rejects the critics' premise; the critics reject the tradition's appeal to lost texts. This is a historical question about sources and no reconciliation principle applies.

notes: Scholarly metadata (labelled, not a side): some modern scholars (e.g. R. Mesquita) have argued that Madhva composed some of these passages; others (e.g. B. N. K. Sharma) defend their authenticity. Which classical opponent first raised the charge was not verified.

question: May the gods (devatās) be worshipped, and must caste and Vedic rites be kept, by one who seeks liberation?

sides.position: The devatās are bound beings who give only worldly fruit; only Parameśvara and his incarnations are to be worshipped; caste and Vedic ritual have no place among seekers.
arguments: The four realities (Sūtrapāṭh).
Liberation from Parameśvara alone.

sides.position: The gods, rites and varṇa duties enjoined by śruti and smṛti bind all; a sect that rejects them is outside dharma.
arguments: Authority of the Veda and smṛti.
sides.note: Known here through the Mahānubhāva account of Hemādri's hostility — reported by the opposing side.

historical_debates.name: Opposition at the Yādava court
historical_debates.accounts: Līḷācaritra
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Cakradhar departs for the north; the community survives, keeping its texts secret.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Mahānubhāvas reject the plurality of worshipful gods that a P2/P3 reconciliation would assume.
candidate_readings: P3-path (iṣṭa-devatā): each worships the chosen form — explicitly rejected by the Mahānubhāvas.
P1-level: devatā-worship as conventional, Parameśvara as ultimate — closer to the Mahānubhāva view but it forbids, not merely ranks, such worship.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Mahānubhāvas insist the devatās are not forms of Parameśvara.

question: Is the root impurity (āṇava mala) a real substance removable only by ritual initiation, or is it ignorance - a contraction of consciousness - removed by knowledge?

sides.position: Āṇava mala is a real, beginningless substance (dravya) that covers the soul's powers of knowing and acting; as a substance it cannot be destroyed by knowledge but only by an act - initiation (dīkṣā) empowered by Śiva - after its ripening; the liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva but remains distinct.
arguments: knowledge cannot remove a substance, as knowing a disease does not cure it
scripture prescribes dīkṣā as the cause of liberation

sides.position: Impurity is ignorance, the cause of the sprouting of saṃsāra (MVT 1.23); ignorance is not the absence of knowledge but its incomplete manifestation (TĀ 1.25-26); knowledge is the sole cause of liberation (TĀ 1.22); the āṇava impurity is consciousness losing its freedom (ĪPK 3.2.4); grace does not depend on the ripening of impurity or on a balance of karma but on the Lord's freedom (TĀ 13); initiation works because it is itself a form of knowledge.
arguments: if mala were a substance, the one consciousness would have a second reality beside it
the same mala is removed in the highly graced by knowledge alone (anupāya)

sides.position: Mala is a substance (dravya); knowledge cannot remove it any more than knowing a cataract cures it; Śiva removes it through the initiation rite.
Āṇava is eternal and is never destroyed; grace makes its power ineffective, like a snake's poison stilled by a mantra; knowledge given by grace (not the soul's own effort) accompanies this.

historical_debates.name: Abhinavagupta's polemic against the dualist Siddhānta (Tantrāloka 1, 13; Mālinīślokavārttika)
historical_debates.accounts: Written polemic, not a recorded face-to-face debate.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition maintains its own view.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the two schools disagree on what mala is.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: 'substance' and 'ignorance' describe the same bondage from an ontological (ritual) and an epistemic (gnostic) standpoint.
P4-stage: Abhinavagupta himself keeps initiation for those whose grace is not intense enough for knowledge alone, so the Siddhānta account could be read as addressed to that stage.
Not reconcilable while one side holds souls eternally distinct and the other holds them identical with Śiva.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Siddhānta rejects any reading that makes mala unreal or knowledge sufficient; the Trika rejects mala as a substance.

notes: Siddhānta side stated from general knowledge of its doctrine (Sadyojyoti, Rāmakaṇṭha II, Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha); text refs for that side are work-level and low confidence - U18 should supply verse anchors. Related: dsp:works-knowledge-grace.

question: What is mastery of the senses (indriya-jaya)?

sides.position: Some: non-addiction (avyasana) to sounds and other objects; some: lawful enjoyment not contrary [to dharma]; others: contact with objects at will; some: cognition of objects free of pleasure and pain in the absence of attachment and aversion.
Jaigīṣavya: non-apprehension alone, from the mind's one-pointedness.
The sūtra and bhāṣya: supreme mastery is that, when the mind is stilled, the senses are stilled with it and need no further effortful means.

historical_debates.name: Doxography of YBh 2.55
historical_debates.accounts: YBh 2.55
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The mastery that follows the stilling of the mind is supreme.

reconciliation.explanation: Vyāsa himself grades the views, calling the last 'supreme' (paramā): they are lower and higher stages of sense-mastery (P4).

question: Are māyā and avidyā the same entity?

sides.position: Identical (Vivaraṇa usage; Saṃkṣepaśārīraka; Vivekacūḍāmaṇi calls māyā 'beginningless avidyā'): one indescribable power, called māyā in its cosmic aspect and avidyā as individual obscuration.
Distinct (Vidyāraṇya): prakṛti with pure sattva is māyā, adjunct of the omniscient Īśvara who controls it; with impure sattva it is avidyā, adjunct of the jīva who is controlled by it.

reconciliation.explanation: Vidyāraṇya's own distinction is of one prakṛti under two aspects (pure/impure sattva), so both sides describe the same entity from the Lord's and the jīva's standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Both sides treat māyā/avidyā as one indescribable principle; the difference is whether the aspects warrant two names.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Some Advaitins insist on a real distinction of function (the Lord is not deluded by māyā; the jīva is by avidyā), which the reconciliation preserves.

question: Is māyā the Goddess's real power (śakti), or an indeterminable ignorance that knowledge sublates?

sides.position: Māyā is the Goddess's own power: she is Mahāmāyā, queen of the supreme Brahman, who transforms herself into mind and the elements, and is 'of the form of knowledge and ignorance'; even ignorance is knowledge, the world is the Lord (Kaula Upaniṣad).
Māyā is the Lord's power but is beginningless ignorance, neither real nor unreal, removed by knowledge of Brahman; duality is mere māyā.
Within Śrīvidyā the Sahasranāma also calls the Goddess 'the substratum of the illusory world', a name read in Advaita terms by Advaita-inclined commentators.

reconciliation.explanation: At the conventional level the world is the Goddess's real play and power; at the ultimate level only she (Brahman) is — the Sahasranāma itself holds both names.
reconciliation.detail: Related to the registry dispute dsp:world-real-or-appearance.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Realist Śākta and Kaula readings (the Kāmakalāvilāsa's real manifestation, the Kaula Upaniṣad's 'the world is the Lord') reject calling the world unreal; Advaita rejects treating māyā as ultimately real power.

question: What does the injunctive form (liṅ etc.) convey, and what prompts a person to act?

sides.position: Kumārila: bhāvanā — the verbal force of the injunction (śābdī) prompting the person's activity (ārthī) toward a result, by means and procedure; the person acts from desire for the result.
arguments: Arthasaṅgraha's analysis of the verbal suffix.

sides.position: Prabhākara: the injunction conveys niyoga, the command / what is to be done (kārya), which itself prompts the qualified person, and is identical with the apūrva.
Maṇḍana Miśra: the injunction conveys that the act is a means to what is desired (iṣṭasādhanatā).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; candidate readings listed.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: prompting (śābdī bhāvanā), command (niyoga) and means-to-the-desired (iṣṭasādhanatā) may describe one injunction from the side of the word, of the hearer's duty and of the goal; the schools themselves argue these are exclusive.

question: How many members does a demonstration (inference for others) need?

sides.position: Five: proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion; together they embody all four means of knowledge. A ten-member view (adding desire to know, doubt etc.) is rejected; stating fewer is the point of defeat 'saying too little'.
arguments: The members correspond to testimony, inference, perception and comparison, their convergence shown in the conclusion (NBh 1.1.1).
NS 5.2.12 (DCS) counts omission of a member as a point of defeat.

sides.position: Fewer members suffice: Dignāga states thesis, reason and example; Dharmakīrti holds that for the competent the reason with its pervasion and presence in the subject is enough, and stating superfluous members is itself a fault in debate.
arguments: The logical force lies in the triple character of the reason, not in the number of statements.

sides.position: Three members suffice — either the first three or the last three (Vedāntaparibhāṣā); Mīmāṃsakas also hold three.
arguments: Recalled from the Vedāntaparibhāṣā's inference chapter (low confidence).

sides.position: The number depends on the listener: two members for the sharp, more (up to ten) for others (Jain logicians, as usually reported).
arguments: Recalled with low confidence.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each side treats the other's practice as a fault in debate.
candidate_readings: P4-stage / P6-upaya: the number of stated members depends on the hearer's capacity — a principle the Jain side states explicitly and Nyāya approaches by distinguishing inference for oneself (no verbal members) from inference for others.
The shared logical core (pervasion plus the reason's presence in the subject) is common to all sides.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya holds five members necessary for a complete demonstration to others; Dharmakīrti holds the extra members superfluous. Neither concedes the other's count.

question: Should the mind be restrained, or — once the truth is known — left unrestrained?

sides.position: Yoga is the restraint (nirodha) of the fluctuations of the mind.
The breath must be bound, for when the breath moves the mind moves and when it is still the yogī becomes like a post (GŚ 38–39).

Once the Kaula is known, restraint of the mind is not to be done; scripture, guru, mantra and Śiva are all free of elaboration (KJN 7.26–27); the mind is not to be grasped nor concentration held — the mind beyond mind is liberated (KJN 13.5).

reconciliation.explanation: The Kaulajñānanirṇaya itself conditions its rule on the stage — 'when the Kaula is known' — so restraint belongs to the practitioner and release to the knower.
reconciliation.detail: KJN 7.26 reads 'mano-rodhaṃ na kartavyaṃ yadā jñātaṃ hi kaulikam'; the Gorakṣaśataka and the Yoga Sūtra address the one still practising.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Not recorded; the Pātañjala tradition would require that release not be claimed before the mind is actually still.

question: Is everything that exists momentary?

sides.position: Yes: whatever exists is momentary, since existence is causal efficacy and an enduring thing could produce its effects neither all at once nor successively; recognition is a construction over a series.
arguments: The argument from causal efficacy (arthakriyā), as reported by Udayana and in NS 3.2.10.

sides.position: No: there is no reason for such a universal rule; things should be accepted as they are seen; causes of arising and destruction are observed only where things arise and perish; recognition shows enduring things and an enduring self; an enduring thing produces effects successively as auxiliaries join it.
arguments: NS 3.2.11–17; 4.1.25–28; Udayana's Ātmatattvaviveka.

historical_debates.name: Udayana's refutations of the Buddhists
historical_debates.accounts: Ātmatattvaviveka; later hagiography presents Udayana as the victor over the Buddhists (tradition's account).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Nyāya tradition: Buddhist doctrine refuted.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: momentariness as the standpoint of modes, endurance as that of substance (Jain).
P1-level: continuity (santāna) as conventionally valid in Buddhist accounts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya rejects momentariness outright, and Buddhist logicians reject endurance; neither accepts the standpoint reading.

question: Is awakening reached by the effortful arousal of kuṇḍalinī, or does it lie in the innate (sahaja), which such practices do not reach?

sides.position: Kuṇḍalinī, lying coiled at the door of Brahman, must be awakened by the fire of yoga with mind and breath and the five seals; then she rises through suṣumṇā and time is cheated (the haṭha position of the Gorakṣaśataka; the Haṭhapradīpikā adds that she wakes 'by the guru's grace').
arguments: GŚ 30–32: awakened by vahni-yoga; seals make one fit for success.
HYP 3.2–3: when kuṇḍalī wakes by the guru's grace the knots are pierced.

sides.position: The Kaula path is twofold: the kuṇḍalī impelled by seals and mantras is 'made' (kṛtaka); the innate (sahaja) abides in samarasa; the Akulavīra is not in any support, channel or breath-practice.
arguments: Akulavīra B.43–45: kṛtaka and sahaja.
Akulavīra A.15–23: not in pūraka, kumbhaka, bindu-piercing...

sides.position: The Amaraughaśāsana (also ascribed to Gorakṣa) denies that liberation is the movement of kuṇḍalinī raised from the root: liberation is where the mind sees the mind in sahaja-samādhi.
arguments: AmŚ 52–53: kuṇḍalinī's movement is a cultivated notion, not liberation.
AmŚ 54: definition of mokṣa.

reconciliation.explanation: The haṭha texts themselves present effortful practice as a stairway to rājayoga/sahaja (HYP 1.1, 4.3–4, 4.114), so arousal of kuṇḍalinī belongs to the stage of practice and sahaja to the goal.
reconciliation.detail: The Akulavīra still counts the 'made' path as a Kaula path (B.43) and the Amaraughaśāsana denies only that kuṇḍalinī's movement is itself liberation (AmŚ 52), not that it has a place; the Haṭhapradīpikā names the goal sahajā and calls talk of knowledge before sahaja hypocrisy. Read by stage, effort is the means and sahaja the end.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Akulavīra's apophatic verses (A.15–23) say the Akulavīra is not found in any practice at all, which resists a merely sequential reading; the haṭha texts would reject any suggestion that the practices are dispensable before sahaja arises.

notes: A Nāth-internal form of dsp:kundalini-effort-grace (U50), to which it should be linked.

question: Do caste duties and Vedic/temple ritual bind the yogī, or are they bondage he must leave behind?

sides.position: For one who knows the supreme there is no caste, sacrifice, fast, pilgrimage, image or rite; worldly and pledge-conduct are 'made bonds'; knowledge alone is to be relied on; the yogī meditates where there is neither temple nor mosque.
arguments: Gorakh Bānī.

sides.position: There are four varṇas and no fifth; each life-stage has its duties, and renunciation comes in due order after the other stages.
arguments: Manu 10.4.

sides.position: Dharma is known from Vedic injunction; its enjoined acts are to be performed.

reconciliation.explanation: The Nāth rejections are spoken of the knower (the 'one in whom this liberation abides') from the ultimate level, while Dharmaśāstra and Mīmāṃsā address the one within the social order — and Dharmaśāstra itself exempts the renouncer from ritual duties.
reconciliation.detail: Within the Nāth corpus the Gorakṣaśataka (v. 3) still calls yoga 'the fruit of the Veda-tree', showing that not all Nāth texts reject the Veda outright.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Akulavīra and Gorakh Bānī call ritual and caste bondage and delusion for all (A.7–10; B.76), not merely unnecessary for the realised; Dharmaśāstra restricts renunciation by varṇa and would not accept the Nāth open recruitment.

notes: Connects to dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50).

question: What is liberation?

sides.position: Isolation (kaivalya): the complete cessation of the threefold suffering; puruṣa has no properties, so liberation is not bliss, motion, annihilation or powers.
arguments: SK 68; SS 1.1, 3.85; liberation is only the destruction of obstacles (SS 6.20); not the manifestation of bliss, destruction of specific qualities, going to a place, total destruction, emptiness, gaining powers or Indra's rank (SS 5.74–83); the praise of liberation as bliss is for the dull (SS 5.68).

sides.position: Liberation is realizing one's nature as Brahman, which is bliss.
arguments: Advaita texts to be cited by U13 (e.g., Taittirīya Up. on Brahman as bliss).

sides.position: Liberation is absolute release from pain (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.22), with the cessation of the self's specific qualities (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).
arguments: Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.22 (recalled).

sides.position: The liberated soul rises to the summit of the world (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.5, recalled).
arguments: Rejected by SS 5.76: the inactive does not go anywhere.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level / P2-standpoint: descriptions by negation (Sāṃkhya, Nyāya: cessation of suffering) vs by affirmation (Advaita: bliss) of a state all agree is beyond saṃsāra.
P7-arthavāda: Sāṃkhya itself reads 'bliss' as figurative praise (SS 5.67–68).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sāṃkhya denies that puruṣa has bliss as a property; Advaita holds bliss is Brahman's nature, not a property.

question: Are the Vedic gods embodied persons, or are they what the mantras name?

sides.position: Yāska reports three views: the gods are like persons (they are praised and addressed as sentient beings with limbs and belongings); they are not like persons (what is seen of them is fire, wind, sun, earth); or both.
arguments: Hymns address the gods as persons; their visible forms are natural powers.

sides.position: For Mīmāṃsā the deity of a rite is what the mantra-word designates as recipient of the offering; embodied gods who eat the offerings and grant rewards are not needed — the rite produces its result (apūrva) itself.
arguments: What the Veda requires for the rite is only the word naming the recipient.

texts.ref: (on the devatā sections; locus from memory)

sides.note: Locus in Śabara recalled only at chapter level (low confidence).

sides.position: The gods are embodied, can take several bodies at once, and are eligible for the knowledge of Brahman (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.26–33, with Śaṅkara).
arguments: Scripture speaks of the gods' forms and of their seeking knowledge (e.g. Indra with Prajāpati).

reconciliation.explanation: Yāska's own third answer — the gods may be 'of both kinds' — treats the personal and the non-personal descriptions as standpoints (as addressed in praise, as seen in nature).
reconciliation.detail: The Mīmāṃsā–Vedānta disagreement remains: it concerns what the Veda requires one to accept, not only how to describe.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsakas reject embodied gods as unnecessary; Vedāntins reject the word-only deity. Neither accepts the other's view as a mere standpoint.

queries: Sabara bhashya devata adhikarana Mimamsa Sutra 9.1
checks.note: Yāska's three views located (Nirukta 7.6–7). Śabara side: the locus left at chapter level in the entry can be specified — Śabara on Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 9.1 (devatādhikaraṇa, adhikaraṇa 4) discusses that the deity does not prompt the rite (na devatā prayojikā); the fuller 'gods are not embodied' argument was not seen in the sources found. Brahma Sūtra 1.3.26–33 is the standard devatādhikaraṇa (not re-checked).

question: Are the cleansing acts necessary before breath-control, and how many are there?

sides.position: (Haṭhapradīpikā) Only those with excess fat or phlegm need the six acts; others should not do them.
('Some teachers', reported in HYP 2.37) All impurities dry up through breath-control alone; the other acts are not approved.
arguments: HYP 2.37

sides.position: (Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā) The cleansing acts are the first of the seven means for everyone; (Haṭharatnāvalī, Haṭhatattvakaumudī) there are eight acts, not six.
arguments: HR 1
HTK aṣṭakarma chapter

reconciliation.explanation: The HYP itself makes the acts conditional on the student's constitution (adhikāra by doṣa), which accommodates both the 'all' and 'none' positions.
reconciliation.detail: The number of acts (six or eight) is a matter of enumeration of variants, not doctrine.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The 'some teachers' of HYP 2.37 reject the acts outright; the reconciliation records that they would not accept them even conditionally.

question: Is the Lord's saving grace without any cause in the soul, or does it take the soul's surrender as its occasion?

sides.position: Grace is causeless (nirhetuka); nothing the soul does earns or occasions it ('mārjāra-nyāya').
arguments: pāratantrya
the Lord's svātantrya

sides.position: Grace is free but takes surrender as its occasion (vyāja), lest the Lord be partial or cruel in not saving all ('markaṭa-nyāya').
arguments: the problem of partiality
scripture's injunction to surrender

reconciliation.explanation: Both deny that surrender earns grace; the Vaṭakalai 'occasion' is not a cause, so the difference concerns the seeker-side description of one divine act.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Teṅkalai reject even 'occasion' on the soul's side; the Vaṭakalai hold that without it the Lord's justice is compromised.

question: How are the Vedic deities and stories to be interpreted — as natural powers, as persons of old narratives, or through the rite?

sides.position: The etymologists: the figures are natural powers — Vṛtra is the cloud; the Aśvins are heaven and earth, or day and night, or sun and moon; the deities are three by station.
arguments: etymology of the names
the three stations of the gods

sides.position: The legend-tellers: the figures are persons of old stories — Vṛtra an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ; the Aśvins two pious kings; Yama and Yamī twins of Saraṇyū.
arguments: the stories told of them

reconciliation.explanation: Yāska himself admits several planes of meaning — 'the flower and fruit of speech are the sacrifice and the deity, or the deity and the self' (Nirukta 1.20).
reconciliation.detail: Later commentators (Durga, Sāyaṇa) read mantras on the planes of the sacrifice, the deities and the self.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school regarded its own reading as primary; the reconciliation is Yāska's plural reading, not an assertion that the schools agreed.

question: Do obligatory (nitya) rites have a result, and why are they performed?

sides.position: They destroy sins done earlier and avert the future demerit that omission would cause; the seeker of release performs them to avoid that demerit.
arguments: Tantravārttika (on MS 1.3.24–29); ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110.

sides.position: They are performed because they are enjoined; the command itself prompts the person whose qualification is simply being alive, without a separate fruit.
Obligatory rites, done without desire, purify the mind and so prepare for knowledge; they do not themselves liberate.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; candidate readings listed.
candidate_readings: P3-path / P4-stage: the same rites are described by their function for different aspirants (avoiding demerit, fulfilling a command, purifying the mind).

notes: The Prābhākara and Advaita sides are from general knowledge (low).

question: Is levirate (niyoga) permitted?

sides.position: Permitted under strict rules: a sonless wife or widow, appointed by the elders, may conceive a son by the husband's brother or a sapiṇḍa (MDh 9.59–63; also earlier Dharmasūtras).
arguments: continuity of the lineage and the ancestral offerings

sides.position: Forbidden: the learned condemn it as fit for animals, introduced under the wicked king Vena (MDh 9.64–68).
arguments: it confuses the classes

reconciliation.explanation: The commentators read Manu's permission and prohibition as belonging to different ages — possible for earlier people, not for those of the Kali age (a verse ascribed to Bṛhaspati is quoted to this effect); later lists count niyoga among kalivarjya practices.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Some commentators instead restrict the prohibition to particular classes or read 9.59–63 as the opponent's view; the Bṛhaspati quotation is known only through commentaries.

notes: Commentarial details from memory (moderate).

question: Are the instruments thirteen or eleven? (a debate among Sāṃkhya teachers)

sides.position: Thirteen: buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and ten external capacities, each inner organ with its own function (classical).
arguments: SK 29, 32–33; functions distinct (SK 23, 24, 27).

sides.position: Eleven: the functions of construction, self-assertion and determination are one; all objects are apprehended in manas (Vindhyavāsin).
arguments: Reported by the Yuktidīpikā on SK 22.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: a counting convention — one inner organ with three functions vs three organs.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kārikā tradition keeps thirteen as its teaching.

question: How many principles (tattvas) are there?

sides.position: Twenty-five principles (prakṛti, its twenty-three evolutes and puruṣa).
arguments: classical Sāṃkhya enumeration

sides.position: Twenty-four with time as the twenty-fifth (Kapila); and, per the Uddhava Gītā, all the seers' counts (9, 11, 5, 3, 26, 25, 7, 6, 4, 17, 16, 13) are right, since the principles enter into one another and each counts by his intention.
arguments: mutual inclusion of the principles (11.22.7-8)
the dispute arises from the Lord's powers and ends with calm (11.22.5-6)

sides.position: Thirty-six principles from Śiva to earth.
arguments: the pure and impure orders of manifestation

reconciliation.explanation: The Uddhava Gītā reconciles the counts itself: the principles interpenetrate, so each enumeration is valid from the speaker's intended standpoint.
reconciliation.detail: Applied beyond the Bhāgavata's own list (to Sāṃkhya's 25 and Śaiva 36) this is an interpretive extension by U06.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Schools that hold their count to be exhaustive (e.g. the Śaiva claim that Sāṃkhya's 25 stops short of the pure tattvas) would not accept that the counts are merely perspectival.

notes: Sāṃkhya and Kashmir Śaiva sides are owned by U09 and U19; U06 records the Bhāgavata's text-internal reconciliation.

question: Is the world false (mithyā), and can the Advaita definitions of falsity withstand Vyāsatīrtha's critique? (The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi controversy)

sides.position: The world is real. None of the five Advaita definitions of falsity is coherent; the inferences from 'perceivable', 'insentient' and 'limited' fail; perception, scripture and above all the witness (sākṣin) establish the world's reality, and what the witness establishes is never sublated. The Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite meaning; the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; liberation is not mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated are graded.
arguments: the subject 'the world in dispute' and the qualifier 'indeterminable' are unestablished
'perceivable' would make the self false too, or prove what both accept
the witness perceives time and the unsublatedness of what it grasps
the scriptures teach difference ('atat tvam asi'); their great purport is Viṣṇu's supremacy
meditation-born realization pleases the Lord; grace liberates

sides.position: The world is mithyā: not ultimately real, since it is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, yet not unreal like a hare's horn, since it appears and functions; Madhusūdana defends each of the five definitions of falsity point by point. Perception shows only empirical existence and does not contradict the Upaniṣadic teaching of non-duality, whose purport is the one Brahman; difference belongs to the empirical order; liberation is the cessation of ignorance by knowledge of identity.
arguments: falsity as 'not the locus of either being or non-being', as 'the counterpositive of a negation in all three times in its own substrate', and the other definitions are defended against Vyāsatīrtha
the empirical reality perception grants is compatible with ultimate sublation
the Upaniṣads' purport, known by the six marks, is non-duality
the witness is pure consciousness and does not certify the ultimate reality of objects

historical_debates.name: The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi exchange
historical_debates.date: 16th–18th c. CE (Nyāyāmṛta early 16th c.; Advaitasiddhi 16th c.; Taraṅgiṇī and Laghucandrikā later)
historical_debates.accounts: A written controversy: Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's point-by-point reply, the Advaitasiddhi; Vyāsa Rāmācārya's Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defending Vyāsatīrtha; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā defending Madhusūdana; further replies on both sides (not all identified in this pass).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition regards its own side as having prevailed; the Mādhva tradition reveres the Nyāyāmṛta and its commentaries, the Advaita tradition the Advaitasiddhi and Laghucandrikā.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides reject the level, standpoint and stage readings.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects all three: difference is 'real in every state, including liberation' (MBTN 1.68–71), the witness shows the world to be unsublated at all times (Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.99–103), and Advaita's two levels of reality are themselves what the Nyāyāmṛta refutes; to call difference 'empirical' is to deny it. Advaita rejects P2 and P4 as reconciliations too: non-duality is not one standpoint among others but the sole reality, and Dvaita's teachings of eternal difference are, for it, errors to be sublated.

candidate_readings.reading: Difference and the world are real at the empirical (vyāvahārika) level, as Advaita itself grants, and non-difference holds at the ultimate level.
Dvaita speaks from the standpoint of the dependent self and its objects, Advaita from the standpoint of the absolute; each is true within its standpoint.
The reality of difference is taught to the seeker; non-difference is realized at the end.

notes: Supplies the Dvaita side of dsp:world-real-or-appearance (U50) as well. The Advaita arguments are summarized from general knowledge of the Advaitasiddhi; U13 should supply text-layer teachings.

question: Do objects exist independently of the mind, or are they only constructions of cognition?

sides.position: The object is common to many minds and stands on its own; it is not constructed by one mind or many.
arguments: The same thing gives pleasure, pain, delusion or indifference to different minds (YBh 4.15).
If it depended on one mind, what would it be when that mind was distracted or stilled? (YS 4.16)
To deny what presents itself by its own power on the strength of conceptual cognition is untrustworthy (YBh 4.14); those who say 'all is mind only' are to be pitied (YBh 4.23).

sides.position: The three worlds are cognition only (vijñapti-mātra); objects appear without external referents, as in dreams.
arguments: Dream objects show that determinate place, time and effects do not require external objects (Viṃśatikā).
Object and cognition are always apprehended together (sahopalambha), so they are not different (Dharmakīrti).
sides.note: Buddhist side stated from Buddhist texts (from memory; refs to check). YBh 4.14–15 reports such views as an opponent.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: Yoga and Yogācāra each explicitly reject the other's account of objects.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Yogācāra's 'mind-only' as a claim about the ultimate, Yoga's realism about the conventional (Yoga would reject the two-level frame).
P4-stage: Yogācāra texts present mind-only as a stage of meditative insight.
Leave distinct: YBh 4.14–23 is an explicit refutation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Vyāsa rejects the Buddhist view as denying what presents itself; Yogācāra rejects external objects.

question: Is devotion directed to the Lord as other, to the one self, or to both? (the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra's three teachers)

sides.position: Kāśyapa (as reported in the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra): devotion is directed to the Lord's majesty (aiśvarya), because he is other than the soul.
arguments: the Lord's otherness (paratva)

sides.position: Bādarāyaṇa (as reported in the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra): devotion is directed to the self as one.
arguments: the texts of identity

sides.position: Śāṇḍilya: devotion is directed to both, on the grounds of scripture and reasoning.
arguments: scripture teaches both difference and identity
reasoning supports both

reconciliation.explanation: The sūtra's own conclusion ('both') treats the Lord-as-other and the self-as-one as two standpoints on devotion's object, each supported by scripture.
reconciliation.detail: This is the text's own reconciliation, recorded as such; it is not extended here to the Vedānta schools' dispute on whether souls are one with or distinct from the Lord (dsp:souls-one-or-distinct).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects any identity-object for devotion; Advaita would take the other-directed devotion as provisional (P1-level) rather than an equal standpoint.

notes: Sūtra numbers (29–31) and wording recalled with low confidence.

question: What are the objects of the bliss (ānanda) and I-am-ness (asmitā) forms of samprajñāta samādhi, and who are the videhas and prakṛtilayas?

sides.position: Vācaspati Miśra: reasoning and reflection have the grasped (gross and subtle elements) as object; bliss has the grasping (the senses, sattva-dominated and pleasant) as object; I-am-ness has the grasper, the sense of 'I' in which the puruṣa is mixed with buddhi; sub-varieties 'with bliss' and 'with I-am-ness' are admitted.
arguments: Maps YS 1.17 onto the grasper–grasping–grasped of YS 1.41.
sides.note: From memory; confirmed only indirectly by Vijñānabhikṣu's report of 'someone' who takes bliss to mean the senses.

sides.position: Bhoja: sānanda is cultivation of the inner organ's sattva tinged by rajas and tamas (grasping-coalescence) — those content there are the 'videhas'; sāsmita is cultivation of pure sattva, mere being — those content there are 'prakṛtilayas'; discernment of the supreme puruṣa is grasper-coalescence.
arguments: Asmitā is not ahaṃkāra.

sides.position: Vijñānabhikṣu: bliss is a joy arising from preponderant sattva, taken as object; it is not the senses; asmitā is awareness with the self alone as object (the individual self or the Supreme Self); there are no 'with bliss / without bliss' sub-varieties.
arguments: The sense organs are gross and would fall under reasoning.
Sūtra and bhāṣya do not mention sub-varieties of bliss.

sides.position: Vyāsa: the bodiless (videha) are gods who experience a quasi-kaivalya with a mind using its own impressions (YBh 1.19); bliss is joy, I-am-ness awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the commentators assign different objects to the upper samprajñāta levels and identify the videhas differently.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: read the accounts as finer or coarser maps of the same ascent.
P2-standpoint: objective (grāhya–grahaṇa–grahītṛ) vs experiential (joy, 'I am') descriptions.
Leave distinct: Vijñānabhikṣu explicitly refutes the senses-as-object view.

question: Can any person be omniscient, in particular directly know dharma?

sides.position: No person perceives dharma: an omniscient is not seen now, cannot be shown to have existed, cannot be established by his own scripture without circularity, and could not be recognized by the non-omniscient; an 'omniscience' by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but perception never grasps tastes by the eye nor the future dharma.
arguments: Perception grasps only the present (MS 1.1.4).
Any excellence of a sense remains within its own domain (ŚV codanā 113–114).
Human statements about the supersensible are like the blind speaking of colours (Śabara).

sides.position: The Buddha is an authoritative person whose knowledge of what is to be abandoned and adopted, with its means, is established; Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla examine the 'seer of supersensible things' at length against Kumārila.
arguments: Knowledge can be perfected by cultivation (Dharmakīrti).
The Mīmāṃsaka's proofs of non-existence of an omniscient are inconclusive.

texts.ref: ch. on the seer of supersensible things

sides.position: The Jina's pure knowledge (kevala-jñāna) directly knows all substances and modes; subtle, hidden and remote things are perceptible to someone (Samantabhadra); Akalaṅka and later Jain logicians answer Kumārila's arguments.
arguments: Knowledge is the soul's nature; with the destruction of the karmas obscuring it, it becomes complete.

sides.position: Īśvara is omniscient; yogic perception, arising from special merit, grasps the supersensible.

texts.ref: ch. 5 (Īśvara as author of the Veda)

historical_debates.name: Tattvasaṅgraha's examination of Kumārila on the omniscient
historical_debates.accounts: a textual debate: the Tattvasaṅgraha and its Pañjikā quote and answer verses attributed to Kumārila
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: each tradition holds its position established

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; candidate readings listed.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Kumārila concedes that an omniscience by all six means of knowledge would not be refuted (ŚV codanā 111); if Buddhist and Jain claims are read as knowledge of what matters for liberation rather than perception of Vedic dharma, part of the dispute narrows — each tradition would reject this narrowing of its own claim.
P3-path: the claims concern different paths (ritual dharma vs liberating insight).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jains and Buddhists affirm full omniscience of their teachers; Kumārila denies any perception of dharma.

notes: The ŚV codanā section names 'the Buddha and others' (v. 130); I found no verse there naming Mahāvīra, though Jain authors reply to Kumārila. Opposing sides summarized from general knowledge (moderate/low).

question: Is the conscious self one or many?

sides.position: Many: each being has its own puruṣa.
arguments: Birth, death and the instruments are allotted separately; beings do not act all at once; the guṇas differ (SK 18; SS 1.149, 6.45).
Vāmadeva and others were liberated while others were not (SS 1.157).
If distribution is by adjuncts, duality returns once they are established (SS 6.46); difference is known from marks (SS 5.61).

sides.position: One: the self is one; apparent plurality comes from limiting adjuncts, like space in pots.
arguments: The self appears as individual selves like space as pot-spaces (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.3–9); this is the objection the Sāṃkhya Sūtra itself states (1.150).

reconciliation.explanation: Sāṃkhya's own reading (SS 1.154): non-duality texts speak of sameness of kind, plurality of number — one and many under different standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Under P2, 'one' names the single nature (pure consciousness) all puruṣas share and 'many' the number of seers; this is how the Sāṃkhya Sūtra reconciles scripture with plurality. It does not claim numerical identity.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaita rejects the reading: the texts of non-duality teach numerical identity of the self with Brahman, and plurality belongs to adjuncts.

question: Are the puruṣas many, or is there one Puruṣa? (MBh 12.294–296, 12.338)

sides.position: The Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers hold that there are many puruṣas and do not accept a single one (as reported in the Mokṣadharma).

The many puruṣas have one source, the universal Puruṣa of the Puruṣa-sūkta (12.338.3–24); the twenty-fifth, awakening, attains the state of the twenty-sixth (12.296.7–12), and Vasiṣṭha contrasts the knowledge of plurality with that of unity.
arguments: 12.338.3: 'as the many have one source'; Brahmā to Rudra 12.338.22–24.

reconciliation.explanation: The Mokṣadharma itself frames the answer as 'many as individuals, one as their source' (12.338.3), a difference of standpoint (the individuals vs their ground).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Sāṃkhya insists on the real plurality of puruṣas; Advaita reads the passages as identity; Dvaita as eternal dependence without identity; none accepts the others' reading as the epic's meaning.

question: Is there one prakṛti for all puruṣas, or one for each? (a debate among Sāṃkhya teachers)

sides.position: One prakṛti, common to all (classical).
arguments: The manifest and pradhāna are common (SK 11); there is only one prakṛti, cause of the three worlds (Gauḍapāda on SK 66); no means of knowledge establishes many (Yuktidīpikā on SK 56).

sides.position: A separate pradhāna for each puruṣa, all following the pradhāna of the great-bodied one (Paurika).
arguments: Reported by the Yuktidīpikā on SK 56.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: cosmic prakṛti (one) vs individual prakṛti as each puruṣa's field of experience (many).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yuktidīpikā rejects Paurika's view for want of proof.

question: Are things established by their own nature (svabhāva), or is everything relative and empty?

sides.position: Things are established by their own nature; the claim that nothing is so established because everything is relative is self-defeating; 'everything is non-existence' is rejected.
Things lack own-nature because they arise dependently; emptiness is not nothingness but dependent origination (Nāgārjuna).
arguments: MMK 15; 24.18 (as usually cited).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Madhyamaka affirms conventional existence of things while denying own-nature ultimately.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya rejects the two-truth frame; Madhyamaka rejects own-nature at the ultimate level.

notes: The link of NS 4.1.37–40 to Madhyamaka is a scholarly reading; the sūtra names no school.

question: Are the five 'M's to be used literally, replaced by substitutes, interiorized, or rejected? (Summary only.)

sides.position: Bliss is Brahman's form in the body and the five 'M's manifest it; they are used in secret worship; when unavailable the daily worship continues without them.
Rejected: the Samaya way admits no Kaula rites or worship of a young woman's triangle.
The right-hand (dakṣiṇa) mode worships with substitutes (anukalpa) or with inner equivalents; the Goddess is worshipped on both right and left paths.

reconciliation.explanation: The traditions themselves assign the modes by qualification and stage, and the Kalpasūtra's continuation of worship without the 'M's shows they are not strictly indispensable.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Samaya school rejects the practice outright, not as a stage; Kaula lineages hold the literal rite superior for the qualified. Restricted content: no procedure recorded.

question: Do Brahma Sūtras 2.2.42–45 reject or uphold the Pāñcarātra?

sides.position: Śaṅkara: they reject the Pāñcarātra doctrine that the jīva (Saṅkarṣaṇa) and mind originate from Vāsudeva, while accepting its worship and meditation.
Rāmānuja: the sūtras state an objection (2.2.42–43) and answer it (2.2.44–45), upholding the Pāñcarātra as authoritative; 'origination' refers to the Lord's forms (vyūhas), not the soul's creation.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: opposite readings of the same sūtras.
candidate_readings: Both agree that the individual soul is not created; they differ on whether the Pāñcarātra teaches its creation.

question: Does the Lord act independently of the karma of souls?

sides.position: The Lord depends neither on karma nor on the soul; he produces the effect at will, all at once or in sequence.
arguments: Those who desire the fruits of action depend on Maheśvara, not he on them (PABh on PS 2.6).
Karma bears fruit when favoured by the Lord's will and can be fruitless without it, as Yayāti's was; beings act because they depend on his will (SDS ch. 6).
The Lord, whose desires are fulfilled, needs nothing karma produces; effects do not arise at once because his power of action follows his will (SDS ch. 6).

sides.position: The Lord's dispensation depends on beings' karma; otherwise he would be partial and cruel; and a Lord who is merely the efficient cause cannot escape either partiality or circular dependence on karma.
arguments: Partiality and cruelty do not belong to the Lord because he depends [on karma] (BS 2.1.34).

A Lord who makes beings low, middle and high would have passion and aversion; if he depends on karma, Lord and karma depend on each other, and beginninglessness does not remove the fault (Śaṅkara on BS 2.2.37).

sides.position: The Lord is the cause who makes human effort fruitful; results do not arise without human action (Nyāya Sūtra 4.1.19-21 as read by its commentators).
arguments: Human action is sometimes seen to be fruitless, so the Lord is a cause; yet without human action there is no fruit; the objection fails because the result is brought about by him.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupatas deny that the Lord depends on karma; Vedānta holds that denying dependence makes him partial.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pāśupata speaks from the divine standpoint (the Lord's freedom), Vedānta and Nyāya from the causal standpoint (karma's regularity); the SDS reply itself gives karma a fruit-bearing role under the Lord's will.
P1-level: at the conventional level karma governs results; the Lord's freedom concerns the level of the ultimate cause.
No reconciliation: the traditions disagree about whether the Lord could act otherwise than karma requires.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Pāśupata tradition explicitly denies that the Lord is karma-dependent (PABh 2.6); Śaṅkara explicitly argues that a karma-independent Lord would be partial.

notes: Nyāya Sūtra side from memory (U11 owns the text); no teaching id created here.

question: Is the Pāśupata (and wider Atimārga) teaching within or outside the Veda?

sides.position: The Pāśupata path is the best of all paths, the true path, others being bad paths; its scripture comes from Maheśvara through the teachers; it uses the Vedic brahma-mantras and is for brahmins; only from the Pañcārtha comes true ascertainment of reality.
arguments: PS 4.16-18; PABh on PS 1.1 (āgama); SDS ch. 6 ('pañcārthād anyato nāsti yathāvat tattvaniścayaḥ').

sides.position: The Vedic Pāśupata vow of the Atharvaśiras is to be followed; the Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula, Vāma and Bhairava scriptures are non-Vedic and were taught for delusion.
arguments: Kūrma P. 2.37.140-146; 1.15.111-113; Śiva P. 7.1.33 (the śrauta Pāśupata vow).

sides.position: All four Māheśvara groups are outside the Veda: they contradict the Vedic Brahman as material and efficient cause and devise āśramas outside the Vedic order.
arguments: Yāmuna, Āgamaprāmāṇya; Rāmānuja, Śrībhāṣya 2.2.35ff.

sides.position: Pāśupata is one of five systems of knowledge (with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra and the Vedas), taught by Śiva Śrīkaṇṭha; Nārāyaṇa is the foundation in all.
arguments: Mahābhārata 12.337.59-64 (Nārāyaṇīya).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupatas claim the highest path; Purāṇic and Vaiṣṇava critics place the Pāśupata scriptures outside the Veda.
candidate_readings: P3-path: the Nārāyaṇīya's own stance - several systems for different temperaments with one foundation.
P4-stage: the Pāśupata presents itself as a state beyond the āśramas for qualified brahmins (atyāśrama).
No reconciliation: the Kūrma Purāṇa and Yāmuna explicitly deny Vedic authority to these scriptures.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kūrma Purāṇa and Yāmuna reject any inclusive reading; the Pāśupata Sūtra calls all other paths bad paths.

question: Is Speech at the level of paśyantī (the grammarians' Word-Brahman) the ultimate reality?

sides.position: The beginningless and endless Brahman is the principle of the Word (śabdatattva), from which the world unfolds; paśyantī, the undivided 'seeing' speech, is the highest level of speech (Bhartṛhari).

What the grammarians call paśyantī is only the knowledge-power at the level of Sadāśiva (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1); the ultimate is Śiva with will, knowledge and action; speech as reflexive awareness is 'supreme speech' (parā vāk) beyond paśyantī (ĪPK 1.5.13).
arguments: paśyantī is sequential and object-related, hence limited
a Word-absolute without the Lord's will and agency cannot account for the world

historical_debates.name: Somānanda's refutation of śabdādvaita (Śivadṛṣṭi ch. 2)
historical_debates.accounts: Written refutation of Bhartṛhari's school, not a face-to-face debate.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The Pratyabhijñā considers the grammarians refuted; the grammatical tradition continued its own view.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: which level of speech is ultimate.
candidate_readings: P1-level: both accept paśyantī as a real level of speech; the Śaivas place parā vāk above it, so the question narrows to whether a level above paśyantī is admitted.
P2-standpoint: Utpaladeva's parā vāk and Bhartṛhari's Word-principle may name the same reflexive consciousness from different standpoints.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Somānanda explicitly denies that paśyantī is the ultimate.

notes: Grammarian side stated at work level (Vākyapadīya 1.1); verse anchors for paśyantī to be supplied by U31.

question: Is the Siddhar Paṭṭiṉattār the same person as Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai?

sides.position: The tradition: one Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam) composed both the Tirumuṟai poems and the Siddhar songs; his life is one story from the eyeless needle to Tiruvoṟṟiyūr.

The scholarly account (recorded as metadata): the Tirumuṟai poet (c. 10th c.) and the author(s) of the Siddhar songs (later, in a different idiom) are distinct; the songs may have more than one author.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: a historical question of authorship to which the eight principles do not apply
candidate_readings: Tradition's account: one poet.
Scholarly account: two or more poets sharing a name and a legend.

question: Is kaivalya (the soul's isolated enjoyment of itself) a permanent state?

sides.position: No: those who attain kaivalya eventually go on to seek the Lord and attain him.
Yes: it is a permanent state at the edge of the eternal realm, from which there is no return.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P5-neyartha: one side's statement read as provisional
both agree kaivalya is inferior to the Lord's service

notes: Positions recalled from secondary accounts; the texts are not cited at section level — check.

question: When a clay pot is baked, is the change of colour in the atoms or in the whole pot?

sides.position: In the atoms (pīlupāka): the pot disintegrates into atoms, which change colour under heat, and a new pot is formed.
arguments: As usually reported in the later literature.

sides.position: In the whole (piṭharapāka): the colour of the pot changes without its being destroyed, heat reaching the parts through the pores.
arguments: As usually reported.
