sides.position: It teaches difference: read 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi', 'you are not that', repeated nine times with examples that show difference (the bird tied to its post, honey from many trees, rivers in the sea); or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control and 'tat tvam asi' as dependence or likeness. Identity contradicts experience ('no one experiences I am omniscient, lord of all') and the conceit of it is the asuras' error.
arguments: experience contradicts identity
no scripture teaches non-difference; all teach difference
the examples illustrate difference
the Nyāyāmṛta refutes the 'impartite meaning' of the sentence

historical_debates.name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha and Vidyāraṇya at Mulbagal
historical_debates.accounts: The Mādhva tradition records a debate on 'tat tvam asi' between Akṣobhya Tīrtha and the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya, with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika: that with the sword of 'tat tvam asi', which separates the Supreme from the soul, Akṣobhya cut down the great forest of Vidyāraṇya.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Mādhva tradition: Akṣobhya prevailed. The Advaita tradition does not accept this account, and the ascription of the verse to Vedānta Deśika is questioned outside the Mādhva tradition.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: all three sides read the same passage with the same exegetical rules and reach opposite purports.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects any reading that makes difference a partial standpoint: the chapter teaches difference and only difference (VTN 1). Advaita holds identity is the sole purport; Viśiṣṭādvaita rejects both unqualified identity and Dvaita's separation of the soul from Brahman's body.

candidate_readings.reading: Identity (of consciousness), inseparability (of body and embodied) and difference (of substance) are each true from a standpoint.
Apply the six marks of purport to the chapter as a whole to decide its purport — a method all three sides accept but apply with opposite results.

notes: A focused exegetical dispute within U50's dsp:souls-one-or-distinct. The Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita sides are summarized from general knowledge; source refs for them are chapter-level.

question: What happens in erroneous cognition (khyāti)?

sides.position: Misplaced apprehension (anyathākhyāti): a real property located elsewhere is apprehended as qualifying the thing before one (silver in mother-of-pearl).
arguments: Tarkasaṅgraha's definition of invalid experience; Gaṅgeśa.

sides.position: Non-apprehension (akhyāti): two cognitions — a perception and a memory — are not distinguished; no cognition is strictly erroneous.
arguments: As usually reported.

sides.position: Apprehension of the indeterminable (anirvacanīyakhyāti): the silver is neither real nor unreal but an appearance produced by ignorance.
arguments: As usually reported.

sides.position: Self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti): cognition's own form is taken as external.
arguments: As usually reported.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Advaita's account presupposes levels of reality that Nyāya does not recognize; within the empirical level the accounts overlap in treating error as a presentation of what is not there.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school's theory of error encodes its ontology; Nyāya rejects the indeterminable and non-apprehension accounts explicitly.

notes: Positions other than Nyāya's are summarized at doxographic level; the owning units should supply texts.

question: What divides the northern (Vaṭakalai) and southern (Teṅkalai) schools of Śrīvaiṣṇavism — the 'eighteen differences' (aṣṭādaśa-bheda)?

sides.position: Surrender is a means the soul performs once, with its limbs, and the occasion of the Lord's grace ('the young monkey clings'); Śrī is all-pervading, of the Lord's rank, and with him the means and goal; the Lord overlooks faults rather than relishing them; scriptural duties bind the surrendered as the Lord's command, and deliberate offences need expiation; kaivalya is not permanent.
arguments: scripture enjoins surrender as a means (Gītā 18.66, the Upaniṣads, Pāñcarātra)
a grace with no occasion would make the Lord partial
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.8.17: as Viṣṇu is all-pervading, so is Śrī
the Catuḥślokī: even the Lord cannot measure Śrī's greatness

sides.position: The Lord alone is the means; surrender is not a means but acceptance fitting the soul's dependence ('the kitten is carried'); grace is causeless; Śrī is the mediator, not the means; the Lord relishes his devotees' faults; duties are kept as service and example, not as means or under threat; the teacher's regard saves; kaivalya is permanent.
arguments: the carama-śloka says 'me alone' and 'abandon all dharmas', including one's own surrender as means
the soul's nature is total dependence (pāratantrya)
the Lord's motherly love (vātsalya) relishes faults
the Tiruvāymoḻi and its commentaries

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools disagree on whether the soul's surrender is a means and on Śrī's rank; see the sub-disputes, some partially reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Teṅkalai speak from the divine standpoint (the Lord alone saves), the Vaṭakalai from the seeker's (surrender is what the seeker does)
P4-stage: the Teṅkalai stress what fits the utterly helpless; the Vaṭakalai what scripture enjoins on the qualified
shared ground: both hold the Lord as siddhopāya, surrender once, no last remembrance needed, release at the end of the body, eternal service
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school regards its points as doctrinal, not a matter of emphasis; neither accepts that the other's view is merely another standpoint.

historical_debates.name: Formation of the two schools
historical_debates.date: 13th–15th c. (doctrine); 17th–19th c. (separate institutions, marks and temple rights)
historical_debates.accounts: Each school traces its view to Rāmānuja through its own teacher-line; later polemical works list eighteen points of difference, whose exact list and author are not reconstructed here.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both continue as living schools; disputes over temple rights (e.g. the forehead mark and invocations at Kāñcī) went to the courts in the colonial period (recalled; low confidence).

notes: The monkey/cat maxims are labels used in the dispute literature and later accounts, not arguments made in these terms by Deśika or Piḷḷai Lokācārya themselves (as far as recalled).

question: Which system — the Vedic Vaikhānasa or the tantric Pāñcarātra — is the proper basis of Viṣṇu temple worship, and must a Vaiṣṇava receive the branding initiation?

sides.position: The Vaikhānasa Sūtra, composed by Vikhanas (Nārāyaṇa/Brahmā), is the first and best of sūtras; its worship is wholly Vedic; Vaikhānasas are Vaiṣṇavas from the womb through the viṣṇubali rite and need no branding; its followers are the highest.
arguments: ten reasons (DHN)
Vedic mantras in every rite
prenatal consecration

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is the Lord's own word, governing the chief self-manifest shrines (Śrīraṅgam, Melkote, Kāñcī), with the five sacraments as the mark of a Vaiṣṇava; only Veṅkaṭādri is excepted.
arguments: the three gems and their temple assignments
authority of the Lord's speech

historical_debates.name: Change of ritual system in Śrīvaiṣṇava temples
historical_debates.accounts: Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition credits Rāmānuja with establishing Pāñcarātra worship in some temples (e.g. Śrīraṅgam); the details are the tradition's account, not verified here.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both systems continue in different temples (e.g. Vaikhānasa at Tirumala).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each community holds its own system to be the better-founded.
candidate_readings: P3-path: two valid ritual paths to the same Viṣṇu, suited to hereditary Vedic eligibility (Vaikhānasa) and to initiatory eligibility (Pāñcarātra).
P4-stage: the Pādma's claim that Pāñcarātra eligibility comes 'at the end' of Mīmāṃsā learning is one side's framing of adhikāra.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Vaikhānasas reject being classed as tantric; Pāñcarātrins reject the view that their system is non-Vedic or lower.

notes: Bhāskararāya (Setubandha intro) quotes a verse saying the Lord taught the Pāñcarātra, Bhāgavata and Vaikhānasa for those fallen from the Veda — a third, Śākta view (recorded in notes only).

question: What is the self common to all men (vaiśvānara)?

sides.position: Each of the five householders and Uddālaka venerates one thing as the vaiśvānara self: the sky, the sun, the wind, space, water or the earth.
arguments: each view had its own fruit

sides.position: Aśvapati Kaikeya: each is only one part (head, eye, breath, trunk, bladder, feet); the vaiśvānara self is to be venerated as the whole, a span in size and beyond measure.
arguments: the whole eats food in all worlds, beings and selves (5.18.1)

historical_debates.name: Aśvapati instructs the six brahmins
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The brahmins accept the king's teaching of the whole

reconciliation.explanation: The text itself treats each view as a true but partial aspect of one whole.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Aśvapati warns that each partial view alone would have brought harm; the parts are not sufficient in isolation.

question: Is inference a valid means of knowledge?

sides.position: No (as reported by opponents): only perception is valid; pervasion cannot be established — perception cannot survey all cases, inference would presuppose inference, and testimony is itself inferential; Jayarāśi's scepticism extends even to perception.
arguments: Reported by opponents (Nyāya and doxographies); Jayarāśi's Tattvopaplavasiṃha is the extant sceptical text.

sides.position: Yes: the alleged deviations of marks (river swelling from damming etc.) involve different marks; the nāstika who uses an example has already given up his position, and one who refutes others must use inference.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: some later Cārvākas (e.g. Purandara, as reported by Kamalaśīla) accepted inference about the perceptible world and rejected only inference to the supersensible — narrowing the disagreement to the unseen (adṛṣṭa, the other world, Īśvara).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya treats the Cārvāka rejection as self-refuting; the Cārvāka side is known only through opponents.

notes: Cārvāka positions are opponents' reports (reported_by_opponent).

question: Is the Pāñcarātra a valid scripture, and does the Brahma Sūtra refute it?

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is invalid: not rooted in the Veda, practised by Sātvatas/Bhāgavatas who are a low temple-serving class, classed by smṛti with heretical systems, and refuted by Bādarāyaṇa.
arguments: no pramāṇa establishes it
Manu names the Sātvata among degraded classes

sides.position: The worship of Vāsudeva by the five daily practices is acceptable, but the doctrine that the soul (Saṅkarṣaṇa) is born from Vāsudeva is refuted, and the system shows contradiction and opposition to the Veda (Śāṇḍilya turning to it after not finding the highest good in the Vedas).
arguments: an originated soul could not be liberated
an instrument (mind) cannot arise from an agent

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is fully valid, spoken by the Lord; the Bhāgavatas are brahmins; the sūtras 42–43 state an objection that 44–45 answer, since the vyūhas are Brahman itself and the Pāñcarātra denies the origination of the soul.
arguments: Yāmuna's Āgamaprāmāṇya
Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya
Vedānta Deśika's Pāñcarātrarakṣā

historical_debates.name: Yāmuna's defence of the Pāñcarātra
historical_debates.accounts: Recorded as a treatise answering the objections point by point (Āgamaprāmāṇya).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śrīvaiṣṇavas hold the Pāñcarātra vindicated.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides read the same sūtras and the same vyūha doctrine differently.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: if the vyūhas are read as forms of the one Lord (Rāmānuja) rather than as the origination of souls (Śaṅkara's report), the Advaitin objection loses its object; Śaṅkara already accepts the worship portion.
P6-upaya: the tradition itself holds different scriptures suited to different devotees.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaitins hold that the Pāñcarātra does teach the soul's origination; Śrīvaiṣṇavas hold that Śaṅkara misreports it.

question: Is varṇa (and eligibility for austerity and teaching) fixed by birth, or made by conduct and qualities?

sides.position: Birth and nature: the varṇas' duties arise from their nature and one should not abandon the work born with one (BhG 18.41–48; 3.35); service is the śūdra's dharma (MBh 12.60.27–28; 5.40.26); Vidura, born of a śūdra womb, will not teach beyond this (5.41.5); in the Rāmāyaṇa the śūdra Śambūka's austerity is held to cause a child's death and Rāma kills him (7.74–76).

Conduct and qualities: one in whom truth, generosity, forbearance, good conduct, non-cruelty, restraint and compassion are seen is a brāhmaṇa (3.177.16); the whole world is of Brahman and came to varṇa by actions (12.181.10); the varṇas were made by guṇa and action (BhG 4.13); knowledge may be taken even from a śūdra (12.306.85); a meat-seller teaches a brāhmaṇa (3.198–206) and a merchant an ascetic (12.253–256); the wise see the same in a brāhmaṇa and a dog-eater (BhG 5.18); women, vaiśyas and śūdras too reach the highest goal (9.32).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the epics record both a birth-based order of duties and eligibility and repeated teachings that conduct and qualities make varṇa and that liberation is open to all.
candidate_readings: P1-level: sameness in the self and in the Lord (BhG 5.18; 9.29) at the ultimate level, varṇa duties at the conventional level
guṇa-karma reading of BhG 4.13 (varṇa by qualities and work) against the birth reading of the classical commentators, who take svabhāva as formed by past lives
bhakti reading: devotion and refuge open liberation to all regardless of birth (BhG 9.32; 18.66), while social duties remain
yuga reading (Rāmāyaṇa 7.74): eligibility for austerity differs by age of the world
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dharmaśāstra and Mīmāṃsā hold birth-based eligibility (adhikāra) for Vedic rites and study; bhakti and reform readings reject birth as a bar to liberation; neither accepts the other's reading as the epics' meaning.

question: Are the four varṇas given by birth from the cosmic Person (RV 10.90.12)?

sides.position: The Puruṣa Sūkta: the brāhmaṇa was the Person's mouth, the rājanya his arms, the vaiśya his thighs, the śūdra born from his feet — the order of society belongs to the cosmic sacrifice.
arguments: The verse and its later use in the Dharmaśāstras as the charter of varṇa by birth.

sides.position: The Buddha mocks the brahmins' claim to be 'born from Brahmā's mouth' when they are seen born from women (Aggañña Sutta), and teaches that one is a brahmin not by birth but by action (Vāseṭṭha Sutta).
arguments: Birth from women is visible to all; conduct, not birth, makes the brahmin.
sides.note: The Pali texts report the brahmins' claim (their paraphrase of the Vedic view).

sides.position: Within the Vedic literature, the seers accepted Kavaṣa Ailūṣa, 'son of a slave woman', when the waters and gods showed him favour (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.19, low confidence).
arguments: Divine favour overrides birth in this episode.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: the Puruṣa hymn speaks of the order of the manifest world (conventional), not of the worth of the self (the hymn also says the Person is all this).
P2-standpoint: cosmic-functional (the body of society) vs personal-ethical (conduct) standpoints.
The traditions themselves (Buddhist, and the bhakti and Siddha critics) reject any reading that keeps birth as the criterion; the Dharmaśāstras reject readings that drop it.

notes: Related to U50's dsp:women-caste-liberation (liberation) — this entry concerns the Saṃhitā verse and the origin of varṇa.

checks.note: RV 10.90.12 and AB 2.19 (Kavaṣa) located; DN 27 and Sn 3.9 are standard loci (not re-checked; SuttaCentral ids dn27, snp3.9).

question: Is the Yoga smṛti refuted by the Vedānta ('etena yogaḥ pratyuktaḥ', Brahma Sūtra 2.1.3)?

sides.position: Brahma Sūtra 2.1.3 declares that Yoga is refuted by the same reasoning as Sāṃkhya; Śaṅkara explains that Yoga is rejected where it teaches an independent pradhāna and a plurality of selves contrary to śruti, while yoga as a discipline and means is accepted.
arguments: Where smṛtis conflict with śruti on the cause of the world, śruti prevails.
sides.note: Summarized from memory; U13 owns these texts.

sides.position: Yoga holds a real prakṛti and many puruṣas (YS 2.17–25, 2.22); commentators answer that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted the independence and reality claimed for pradhāna and a real difference of consciousness, not yoga as meditative cultivation, which the Gītā holds higher (Nārāyaṇatīrtha).
arguments: The yoga that is refuted is doctrinal, not practical.
Vijñānabhikṣu likewise harmonizes Yoga with Vedānta.

reconciliation.explanation: Both Śaṅkara's reading of BS 2.1.3 and the late Yoga commentators accept yoga as a path of practice while leaving the metaphysical disagreement standing (P3).
reconciliation.detail: Not reconciled: the reality and independence of pradhāna and the plurality of puruṣas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Yoga (Vyāsa, Vācaspati in his Yoga commentary) does not concede that its dualism is refuted; Advaita does not concede that it is true.

question: Is the killing prescribed in Vedic ritual an injury (hiṃsā) that brings demerit?

sides.position: No: the injury prescribed by the Veda is non-injury, for dharma shone forth from the Veda (MDh 5.44); animals were created for sacrifice.
arguments: the Veda is the sole authority on dharma

sides.position: Abstention is better: meat cannot be had without injury, killing does not lead to heaven (MDh 5.48); eating meat is natural activity, abstention bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).
arguments: the nature of meat
the fruit of nivṛtti

sides.position: The Vedic means are impure (aviśuddhi) because they involve killing; their fruit is also perishable (Sāṃkhyakārikā 2 as its commentators explain).
arguments: the general prohibition 'do not harm any being' is not cancelled by the special injunction

sides.position: Injury to living beings is never dharma, whether in ritual or not; the Śramaṇa traditions reject animal sacrifice.
arguments: non-injury as the highest dharma

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: Mīmāṃsā: a specific injunction removes the general prohibition for its own case (no demerit)
Sāṃkhya: both apply — the rite yields its fruit and the killing its demerit
P4-stage reading of MDh 5.56: ritual meat is permitted at the level of pravṛtti, abstention is the higher nivṛtti
yuga-dharma: later authorities forbid animal (cow) sacrifice in the Kali age
Brāhmaṇa substitution: the sacrificial essence passed from animals into rice and barley (ŚB 1.2.3.6–9)

notes: Sāṃkhya and Jain sides summarized at text level from memory; their own units hold the verse-anchored teachings.

question: Are the Śākta tantras Vedic and authoritative?

sides.position: Only the five Śubhāgamas, which teach the Vedic Samaya way, are fully authoritative for the twice-born; the sixty-four tantras aim at worldly powers, deceive even the learned, are far from the Vedic path and meant for others; the eight Candrakalā tantras are mixed.

Śrīvidyā is itself taught in śruti — the Tripurā, Bhāvanā, Kaula and Bahvṛca Upaniṣads — and the Gāyatrī is the Śrīvidyā; the Kalpasūtra calls itself a great Upaniṣad whose study makes one the performer of all sacrifices; the vidyā is hidden within all schools while the Veda is public. Bhāskararāya defends this with Mīmāṃsā reasoning.
Texts not accepted by those who know the three Vedas — including the Pāśupata and Pāñcarātra āgamas — have no authority as sources of dharma.

historical_debates.name: Bhāskararāya's defence of Śrīvidyā at Kāśī
historical_debates.accounts: The Bhāskaravilāsa is said to tell of his victories over Vedic critics (from memory; not checked).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Victory for Bhāskararāya (the tradition's account).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides disagree about which texts are Vedic, not only about who may use them.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: all sides already distribute texts by eligibility (adhikāra); authority could be read as relative to the qualified practitioner.
P7-arthavāda: the Kalpasūtra's claim to be a great Upaniṣad and the Saundaryalaharī's disparagement of the sixty-four tantras may be praise and blame rather than doctrine.
P5-neyārtha: Lakṣmīdhara's classification may be provisional teaching for Vedic householders.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsakas deny any non-Vedic source of dharma; Lakṣmīdhara denies the sixty-four tantras for the twice-born; Kaula Śrīvidyā denies that its tantras are outside the Veda.

question: May one kill in battle as one's own dharma — and what of non-violence as the highest dharma?

sides.position: Arjuna: killing kinsmen is sin, destroys family dharma and leads to hell; it is better to be killed unresisting or to live by begging (BhG 1.31–47; 2.5).

Kṛṣṇa: the self neither slays nor is slain; for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a righteous war; acting without ego one does not slay even in slaying; the warriors are already slain by Time (BhG 2.18–38; 11.32–34; 18.17).
Non-violence is the highest dharma (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116; Tulādhāra 12.253–256; Vicakhnu 12.257); Satyavat argues against even capital punishment (12.259).
The meat-seller: no one lives without harming beings — even farmers and non-violent ascetics — so one's own inherited work done rightly is dharma (MBh 3.199).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the epic records both the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war and non-violence as the highest dharma.
candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): the kṣatriya's duty belongs to his station; the ideal of non-violence to renunciants and ekāntins
P1-level: 'it neither slays nor is slain' (2.19) at the ultimate level, while the conventional duty of the warrior stands
action without ego and attachment does not bind (18.17)
allegorical reading of the battle as the inner struggle (Gandhi; recent) — rejected by the classical commentators, who read the war literally
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jain and Buddhist traditions (outside this unit) reject killing as anyone's own dharma; the classical commentators reject the allegorical reading.

question: Does liṅga-initiation abolish caste and pollution distinctions among devotees?

sides.position: Yes: among liṅga-wearers there is no caste — Basava is the son of a cobbler's house and every devotee is 'ours'; the five pollutions do not apply; the intercaste marriage of Haraḷayya's son and Madhuvarasa's daughter enacted this.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.
The Kalyāṇa narrative.

sides.position: Devotion, not birth, makes the bhakta; the māheśvara drops jāti-dharmas opposed to the liṅga; at union brāhmaṇa and outcaste are alike and the realized are untouched by pollution — yet the practitioner eats with twice-born of his own jāti on the path, and the ordering of varṇa and āśrama is twofold (Śiva's and Brahmā's).
Varṇa and the rules of purity bind all; marriage across varṇa in the pratiloma direction is forbidden — the objection of the orthodox in the Kalyāṇa narrative (as reported in Vīraśaiva hagiography).
arguments: Dharmaśāstra rules of varṇa and marriage (general).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, commensality rules for practitioners (9.29) and equal vision for the realized (14.19–20) are assigned to different stages by the text itself (5.22–23); between the vacana strand, the SSM and dharmaśāstra orthodoxy the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers reject any stage-based retention of caste among devotees; dharmaśāstra orthodoxy rejects the Vīraśaiva equality claim.

notes: Contributes the Vīraśaiva sides to the wider dsp:women-caste-liberation (owned by U50).

question: Did the Vīraśaiva/Liṅgāyata tradition begin with Basava and the śaraṇas of twelfth-century Kalyāṇa, or is it a beginningless Śaiva dharma renewed in every age by the five ācāryas?

sides.position: Vīraśaiva dharma is anādi: Śiva taught it in the later portion of the Āgamas and to the Goddess and Nandin; Reṇuka emerged from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki and taught Agastya; the five ācāryas appear from liṅgas in every yuga and founded the five pīṭhas. Basava is a great devotee and reviver within this stream.
arguments: The SSM's own frame of transmission (1.28–31; 3.83–87; 4.1).
The Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' teach Vīraśaiva doctrine in their uttara-bhāga (5.14).
The Tattvapradīpikā already names the Pañcācārya lineage and links Siddharāma to Revaṇasiddha.

sides.position: The tradition was inaugurated by Basava with Allama Prabhu, Cennabasava, Akka Mahādēvi and the śaraṇas in Kalyāṇa; the vacanas are its founding scripture; the Pañcācārya narratives and the Sanskrit Āgamic framing come later.
arguments: The vacanas and the earliest hagiographies (Harihara's ragaḷes) centre on Basava and the śaraṇas.
The Śūnyasampādane presents Allama and Basava's Anubhava Maṇṭapa as the tradition's origin-scene.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: the two accounts differ on a historical question (who began the tradition and when) to which the eight principles do not apply as a hermeneutic
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pañcācārya account speaks from the standpoint of the dharma's eternal transmission, the śaraṇa account from that of its historical renewal — each side rejects this as diminishing its account.
Two streams — a Śaiva ācārya/maṭha stream and the Kalyāṇa devotional movement — later merged (a scholarly hypothesis, labeled; it also invokes a Kālāmukha background, see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva).
Basava as reviver of an older dharma (the Pañcācārya reading) — rejected by the śaraṇa strand.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each strand holds its account as historical fact, not as a standpoint.

notes: Scholarly account (labeled): the śaraṇa movement is datable to the 12th c.; the Sanskrit Pañcācārya literature is attested later and its dating is debated; some scholars also point to pre-Basava Kannada Śaiva devotees (Dēvara Dāsimayya, Ēkānta Rāmayya) and to Kālāmukha antecedents.

question: Is Śiva to be worshipped in temples and installed images (the fixed), or in the personal liṅga and the living devotee (the moving)?

sides.position: Installed liṅgas in temples are proper seats of Śiva's worship for the community (temple worship as taught in the Āgamas).
arguments: Āgamic temple ritual (general; U08/U18 supply texts).

sides.position: The fixed shall perish, the moving endures; the body is the temple; to feed the stone snake and drive off the living devotee is hypocrisy.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.

sides.position: Graded: palm-worship of the iṣṭaliṅga excels pedestal worship; the inner liṅga excels stone liṅgas and clinging only to the outer is delusion; yet the nirmālya of fixed liṅgas is not to be used and fixed liṅgas are to be protected.

reconciliation.explanation: Within the Vīraśaiva texts the forms of worship are graded by stage (outer liṅga for all, inner for the advanced; 6.48; 15.44); vis-à-vis Āgamic temple Śaivism the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The vacana strand does not treat temple worship as a lower stage but rejects it; temple Śaivism does not accept the iṣṭaliṅga as replacing public worship.

question: What authority do the Veda and the Āgamas have for Vīraśaivas?

sides.position: The Veda is the chief authority; the Śaiva Siddhānta Āgama is 'made of the Veda', one with it in meaning and as authoritative; the Vīraśaiva doctrine is taught in the Āgamas' later portion and agrees with Veda and Vedānta — though sacrifices and austerities without Śiva-devotion are fruitless and not worth a fraction of liṅga-worship.
arguments: SSM 5.3–14 on authority.
SSM 6.58–61 reads the Ṛgveda as enjoining liṅga-wearing.
SSM 8.36–43; 11.48–49; 15.30–36 subordinate sacrifice to devotion.

sides.position: Scripture is to be tested by experience: Basava will put the Veda to the touchstone, fetter the śāstras and cut the nose of the Āgamas; the śaraṇas' vacanas and anubhava are the authority.
arguments: Basava's vacana 'Vēdakke oregalla kaṭṭuve'.
Basava's refusal of the sacred-thread rite (hagiography).

sides.position: The Ārādhyas wear the liṅga and worship Śiva exclusively while keeping the sacred thread and Vedic rites.
arguments: Tradition-account of the Ārādhya community (low confidence).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, reverence for the Veda and the subordination of Vedic rites to liṅga-worship are reconciled by stage (5.22–23; 9.39–40; 15.30–36); between the SSM and the vacanas the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Candidate for the inter-strand question: P7-arthavada (the vacana's 'touchstone' as praise of devotion rather than doctrinal rejection) — a reading the Basava-centred strand rejects.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers hold the vacana's rejection of Vedic authority to be meant literally; the Ārādhya and Pañcācārya positions hold Vedic authority non-negotiable.

question: Is the self the body (as seen in its reflection)?

sides.position: Virocana, for the asuras: the bodily self alone is to be worshipped and served here; by serving it one wins both worlds — hence the dead are adorned with food, clothes and ornaments.
arguments: the person seen in the eye and in water is the adorned body (ChU 8.8.1-3)

sides.position: Prajāpati's final teaching as received by Indra: the body is mortal, the base of the immortal bodiless self, which is free from evil, old age, death and sorrow and appears in its own form in the highest light.
arguments: the reflection perishes with the body (8.9.1)
the bodiless is untouched by pleasure and pain (8.12.1)

historical_debates.name: Indra and Virocana with Prajāpati
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Virocana's view is 'the upaniṣad of the asuras'; Indra reaches the self

reconciliation.explanation: The body-self is the first of four successive teachings given to a student; Virocana stopped at the first stage, Indra went on to the last.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: ChU 8.8.4 says those who hold this doctrine will perish; the P4 reading claims only that it is a provisional stage, never a valid final view.

question: The rivalry of the priestly houses of Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha

sides.position: Viśvāmitra's house: Viśvāmitra is priest of the Bharatas and of Sudās (RV 3.33, 3.53); the closing imprecations of 3.53 are traditionally taken as aimed at Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha's descendants do not recite them.
arguments: The Bharatas' crossing of the rivers by Viśvāmitra's word; the imprecation verses.

sides.position: Vasiṣṭha's house: Vasiṣṭha is Sudās's priest in the Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18, 7.33) and swears 'may I die today if I am a sorcerer', against one who falsely called him so (7.104.15).
arguments: Victory of Sudās through the Vasiṣṭhas' prayers.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a rivalry of lineages, remembered differently by each house and by the epics.
candidate_readings: The epic account (Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa) resolves it by Viśvāmitra's tapas and Vasiṣṭha's final acknowledgement of him as brahmarṣi — a P4-stage reading (change of standing through attainment).
The two houses served one king at different times (a historical, non-doctrinal reading).
The attributions of the imprecations and of the sorcery charge are commentarial and may not concern Vasiṣṭha at all.

notes: The traditional attribution of 3.53.21–24 and 7.104 to this rivalry is recalled from commentarial literature with moderate-low confidence.

checks.note: The low-confidence traditional attributions are confirmed in Sāyaṇa: on 3.53.21 the four verses are 'vasiṣṭhadveṣiṇyaḥ', Viśvāmitra cursed Vasiṣṭha with them and 'the Vasiṣṭhas do not listen to them'; on 7.104.15 the verse is Vasiṣṭha's oath against being called a rākṣasa.

question: Is the Vrātya an exalted cosmic figure or an outsider to be brought into the Vedic fold?

sides.position: The Atharvaveda's Vrātya book exalts the Vrātya: he stirs Prajāpati, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, and a king should honour the knowing Vrātya above himself.
arguments: AVŚ 15 throughout.

sides.position: The Sāmaveda Brāhmaṇa tradition prescribes the vrātyastoma rites by which vrātyas — people living outside Vedic rules — are admitted to Vedic society.
arguments: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 17.1–4 (reference from memory).
sides.note: Locus recalled from memory (moderate-low); U02 owns the Brāhmaṇas.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Atharvaveda speaks of an ideal, cosmic Vrātya 'who knows thus'; the Brāhmaṇa of actual vrātya groups.
P7-arthavāda: the exaltation of the Vrātya is praise of the knower, not a description of vrātya groups.
Commentators (e.g. Sāyaṇa) take the Vrātya of AVŚ 15 to be a learned, revered figure or the Supreme (recalled, low confidence).

notes: Scholarly hypotheses linking the vrātyas to early Rudra-worshipping or ascetic groups are metadata only (see brw:vratya-and-saiva-ascetics).

checks.note: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 17.1–4 vrātyastomas located (hīnā vā ete hīyante ye vrātyāṃ pravasanti …) — the locus from memory is exact. Sāyaṇa on AVŚ 15: introduces vrātya as one without upanayana, yet on 15.1.1 calls the Vrātya 'vidvattama, mahādhikāra, puṇyaśīla, viśvasaṃmānya' — confirming 'a learned, revered figure'; the 'or the Supreme' alternative not seen.

question: May one renounce directly, at any stage of life, or only after passing through the householder's duties?

sides.position: Renounce on the very day dispassion arises, from studentship, household or forest; true renunciation is inner union of jīva and Self.
arguments: Jābāla 4: 'yad ahar eva virajet tad ahar eva pravrajet'
Nāradaparivrājaka 3: renunciation without dispassion leads to a fall; the self-controlled may renounce unmarried
Maitreya 2.17: renunciation is not abandoning rites but union with the Self

sides.position: Renunciation comes in due order, after the three debts (study, offspring, sacrifice) are paid; seeking liberation before paying them leads downward.
arguments: Manusmṛti 6.35–37 on the three debts
the Kuṇḍikā and Kaṭharudra themselves describe renunciation after studentship, marriage and sacrifices

historical_debates.name: Brahmasūtra 3.4.18–20: are the other stages of life enjoined?
historical_debates.accounts: The sūtras report Jaimini's view that scripture only mentions the other stages without enjoining them and Bādarāyaṇa's that they are to be practised; Śaṅkara, commenting, cites the Jābāla's rule on renouncing directly.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita: renunciation is enjoined and may be taken directly.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts tie the timing to the renouncer's qualification: in due order for most, at once for one of intense dispassion; and the Maitreya distinguishes outer ritual renunciation from inner renunciation.
reconciliation.detail: The Nāradaparivrājaka itself says that renouncing without dispassion causes a fall, which grounds the adhikāra reading (P4); the Maitreya's definition places true renunciation on the level of knowledge (P1).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Ritualists (Mīmāṃsā) hold that lifelong Vedic duties cannot be set aside; the Jābāla's partisans hold that dispassion alone decides, whatever one's stage.

question: Which 'Bhāgavata' is the Mahāpurāṇa of the lists - the Śrīmad (Viṣṇu) Bhāgavata or the Devī Bhāgavata?

sides.position: The Śrīmad Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa: it begins with the Gāyatrī-marked verse, contains Vṛtra's slaying and has 18,000 verses (Matsya 53.20-22), calls itself the essence of all Vedānta and the fruit of the Veda-tree.
arguments: the Matsya definition fits it
its own verse count (12.13.9)
its opening 'dhīmahi' evokes the Gāyatrī

sides.position: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'; the Viṣṇu Bhāgavata is an Upapurāṇa (some polemicists alleged it was composed by Vopadeva).
arguments: it too has 18,000 verses and treats the Gāyatrī and the slaying of Vṛtra
the Devī Bhāgavata's own list of Purāṇas

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides apply the same Matsya definition to different texts; no principle decides identity of a title.
candidate_readings: P3-path: each is the 'Bhāgavata' for its community of worshippers (Vaiṣṇava, Śākta) - both traditions would reject this as evading the question.
The lists' 'Bhāgavata' predates both extant texts and the title was later claimed by each.
Scholarly metadata: modern scholars date both later than the lists' earliest layers.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Vaiṣṇava commentators insist on the Śrīmad Bhāgavata alone; Śākta authors on the Devī Bhāgavata.

historical_debates.name: pamphlet controversy over the Bhāgavata's status
historical_debates.accounts: Polemical tracts on both sides (titles such as 'Durjanamukhacapeṭikā' are reported; authorship and dates not verified in this sweep).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: each side claims victory

question: Which deity is the supreme Brahman — Śiva, Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa, or the Goddess?

sides.position: Śiva/Rudra is supreme: he alone was in the beginning; as Śarabha he subdued Nṛsiṃha; Śiva alone is to be meditated on.
arguments: Atharvaśiras 1
Śarabha
Atharvaśikhā

sides.position: Nārāyaṇa is supreme: Brahmā and Rudra are born from him; Nārāyaṇa alone existed in the beginning.
arguments: Nārāyaṇa 1
Mahā 1

sides.position: The Goddess is supreme: she alone was in the beginning and gave birth to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra.
arguments: Bahvṛca 1–3
Devī 1–2

reconciliation.explanation: The identity Upaniṣads read the names as one reality (Viṣṇu the heart of Śiva, Śiva of Viṣṇu), and each sectarian text's supremacy claim can be read as praise of the chosen deity.
reconciliation.detail: Skanda 8–9, Rudrahṛdaya 1–5 and Kaivalya 8–10 identify the gods; the chosen-deity principle (P3) and the arthavāda reading of exaltation over rivals (P7) account for the sectarian texts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sectarian theologians deny that their supremacy claims are mere praise; the Śarabha's subjugation of Nṛsiṃha is rejected by Vaiṣṇavas, and Śaiva authors reject the Mahā's account of Śiva's birth from Nārāyaṇa.

question: Which aim of life is foremost — dharma, artha, kāma, their combination, or liberation?

sides.position: The combination, with dharma weightiest: the settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224); dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra (YS 2.21); self-knowledge leads to the supreme good (MDh 12.85).
arguments: dharma as the root of the others' legitimacy
liberation after the debts are paid

sides.position: Artha is foremost, for dharma and kāma are rooted in artha (Kauṭilya).
arguments: the world's livelihood depends on wealth

sides.position: The three are to be pursued in balance over the stages of life, each earlier weightier, artha first for a king; kāma needs its own śāstra.
arguments: the allotment of aims to ages of life

sides.position: Lokāyatikas (as reported by Vātsyāyana): dharma should not be practised, its fruit being future and doubtful — better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow.
arguments: uncertainty of unseen fruit

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves distribute the aims over the stages of life and over active and quiescent paths (Kāmasūtra 1.2.2–4; MDh 12.88–90).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kauṭilya still holds artha foremost; the Lokāyata view (known only as reported) rejects dharma altogether; for Manu the triad is subordinate to self-knowledge.

historical_debates.name: The Pāṇḍavas' discussion of the three aims
historical_debates.accounts: In the Śāntiparvan (MBh 12.161, as usually cited) Vidura, Arjuna, Nakula–Sahadeva and Bhīma each argue for an aim and Yudhiṣṭhira points beyond them.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: recorded in the Mahābhārata (U05); details from memory, to be checked

question: What makes one a brāhmaṇa — birth, body, learning, action, or realization of the Self?

sides.position: Not jīva, body, birth, learning, action or dharmic deeds; the brāhmaṇa is one who has realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults; caste belongs to convention.
arguments: Vajrasūci: seers born of deer, jackal, anthill, fisherwoman
Nirālamba: caste is not of skin, blood, flesh or bone; imagined for convention

sides.position: Varṇa is by birth, with conduct and rites determining standing within it.
arguments: the Vajrasūci's own opening states the received view: 'of the four castes the brāhmaṇa is chief, say the Vedas and smṛtis'

reconciliation.explanation: The Nirālamba itself places caste in convention (vyavahāra) and the true brāhmaṇa at the level of realized truth, so both can hold on different levels.
reconciliation.detail: Read by levels of truth, birth-caste operates in conventional social and ritual life, while the Vajrasūci defines the brāhmaṇa by realization.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dharmaśāstra authors would not accept that varṇa is merely imagined; the Vajrasūci claims its definition is the intent of all scripture, not merely a higher level.

notes: Related registry dispute: dsp:women-caste-liberation. The Buddhist Vajrasūcī makes a parallel argument; see brw:buddhist-vajrasuci.

question: Who may learn and recite the Veda?

sides.position: The recitation lineages transmit the Veda to the initiated (upanayana) twice-born; the Purāṇa says the triple Veda is not for the hearing of women, śūdras and lapsed twice-born, for whom Vyāsa composed the Mahābhārata (Bhāgavata 1.4.25); the Brahma Sūtra denies śūdras the right to Vedic study (1.3.34–38).
arguments: Eligibility (adhikāra) follows initiation.

sides.position: The Saṃhitās themselves record women seers (ṛṣikās) of hymns, a maiden's brahmacarya (AVŚ 11.5.18), a seer 'son of a slave woman' accepted by the gods (AB 2.19), and a verse speaking auspicious speech to brahmin, rājanya, śūdra, ārya, one's own and the stranger (VS 26.2).
arguments: The seers' own record.

sides.position: Dayānanda (recent): Vedic study and initiation are open to all, women and men of every birth, citing VS 26.2.
sides.note: Recent (post-1800).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): the tradition's own frame — different texts and practices (Veda; epic and Purāṇa; the divine name) for different eligibilities — which the restricted parties and later reformers reject when eligibility is by birth.
Historical: women's Vedic study (brahmavādinīs) is attested in the Saṃhitās and early sūtras and was later restricted.
VS 26.2 read narrowly (addressing all with auspicious words at the rite) or broadly (teaching the Veda to all).

notes: Related to U50's dsp:women-caste-liberation.

checks.note: All textual loci located or web-confirmed (Bṛhaddevatā 2.82–84). Brahma Sūtra 1.3.34–38 (apaśūdrādhikaraṇa) is standard (not re-checked).

question: Who is eligible to renounce?

sides.position: Restrictive: lists of the ineligible (the impotent, fallen, deformed, heretics, the unlearned and others); the ineligible may renounce only when at the point of death.
arguments: Nāradaparivrājaka 3.1–11
Sannyāsa 2.1–5

sides.position: Open: anyone dispassionate — with or without vows or fires — may renounce; eligibility is having found desires like vomit.
arguments: Jābāla 4
Maitreya 2.18–20

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the restrictive lists govern ritual renunciation, the open statements define the renouncer by inner dispassion; whether one limits the other is not settled here.

candidate_readings.reading: P4-stage / P1-level: rules for ritual (krama) renunciation vs the knower's inner renunciation open to anyone dispassionate
The Nāradaparivrājaka's own clause that the ineligible who have renounced are still fit for the great saying

notes: Related registry dispute: dsp:women-caste-liberation. The texts assume male renouncers.

question: Is a whole (avayavin) something real over and above its parts?

sides.position: Yes: the whole is a new substance inhering in its parts, perceived as one; otherwise nothing could be perceived (atoms being imperceptible) and a thing could not be held or pulled as one.
arguments: Perception of wholes; the imperceptibility of atoms; holding and pulling (NS 2.1.31–37).
Objections that a whole can reside in its parts neither wholly nor partly are answered (NS 4.2.4–17).

sides.position: No: only the parts (ultimately momentary particulars) are real; the 'whole' is a conceptual construction over an aggregate.
arguments: A whole can occur in its parts neither wholly nor partially (cf. the pūrvapakṣa of NS 4.2.7–10).
What is analysed away by the intellect is not ultimately real (cf. NS 4.2.26).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Jain distinction of a standpoint of the enduring whole (dravyārthika) from one of parts and modes (paryāyārthika) would treat the two as partial views.
P1-level: Buddhist two-truth doctrine allows wholes conventional (not ultimate) reality.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya denies that the whole is merely a standpoint or conventional; the Buddhist logicians deny its reality. Neither accepts the P2 reading.

question: May (or should) a widow follow her husband onto the pyre?

sides.position: The widow's dharma is lifelong chastity and restraint (MDh 5.156–160); Medhātithi (on Manu) holds that following the husband in death is self-destruction, not dharma, comparable to a rite performed to harm.
arguments: the prohibition of taking one's own life
Manu's silence on the practice

sides.position: It is permitted as an option: chastity or ascending the pyre (Viṣṇusmṛti 25.14); the Mitākṣarā (on YS 1.86) defends it as a meritorious optional act.
arguments: an explicit smṛti option
the promised reward

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: Medhātithi's Mīmāṃsā argument that a rite motivated by desire and involving killing is not dharma
the Mitākṣarā's reading as an optional (kāmya) act
later kalivarjya-style prohibitions and the Śākta tantras' prohibition (outside this unit)

notes: Recorded neutrally as a debate within Dharmaśāstra; commentators' locators given at section level from memory (low).

question: Is this world a 'frame of illusion' to be seen through, or a 'mansion of mirth' to be enjoyed in the Lord?

sides.position: (Rāmprasād) 'This world is a frame of illusion' — the mind should not be deceived by it but turn to the Mother.
(Āju Gosāi, a Vaiṣṇava contemporary, in the tradition's account) 'This world is a mansion of mirth' (majār kuṭi), where one eats, drinks and makes merry with the Lord.

historical_debates.name: Rāmprasād and Āju Gosāi's song-exchange
historical_debates.accounts: Bengali oral tradition; later cited by Ramakrishna (U52).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Remembered as a friendly contest of songs.

reconciliation.explanation: The same world is a trap to the one still bound and a mansion of mirth to the one who has realised the Lord (Mother) in it — the reading given in the Ramakrishna tradition.
reconciliation.detail: Recorded as the later tradition's reconciliation (U52 to anchor in the Kathāmṛta); both songs are quoted there.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded; the exchange is remembered as good-humoured.

question: What place, if any, has yogic discipline (haṭha, aṣṭāṅga, kuṇḍalinī) on the Sant path of the Name?

sides.position: None as a means: sahaj is best — no closing of eyes, stopping of ears or mortification; the yogī dyes his clothes, not his mind; the Name and love suffice.
arguments: forced yoga breeds pride and display
the Lord is found by love and the Name

sides.position: Sundardās teaches aṣṭāṅga and haṭha yoga (postures, breath, cakras, the serpent power) as a stage within the Sant path, below devotion and knowledge.
Caraṇdās teaches the eight limbs of yoga to his disciples as a support of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the guru.
Only the yoga of the sound current, beginning at the eye centre, is needed; haṭha and kuṇḍalinī work on the lower centres is unnecessary and hazardous; surat-śabd yoga is the crown of yogas.

reconciliation.explanation: Sundardās and Caraṇdās themselves place yoga as a preparatory stage (P4) under the Name and devotion; temperaments differ (P3).
reconciliation.detail: Claims only that the Sant tradition contains this graded view; it does not claim that Kabīr's verses or Sant Mat accept yoga as a stage.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kabīr's verses reject forced yoga outright; Sant Mat rejects lower-centre yoga as unnecessary; for the Nāth side of the wider question see dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21).

notes: Intra-Sant counterpart of dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21, Nāth vs Sant), which records the Kabīr–Gorakh goṣṭhī.

question: Is knowledge alone sufficient for liberation, or must bodily yoga accompany it?

sides.position: Yoga and knowledge together: knowledge without yoga cannot liberate, and the mere knower is reborn until his body is 'ripened' by yoga.
arguments: Yogatattva 14–15

sides.position: Knowledge alone gives kaivalya; bodily yoga is for the unawakened; realization is not samādhi or yogic attainment but oneness with Brahman.
arguments: Muktikā prose: not by works, Sāṃkhya, yoga or worship
Tejobindu 1.33: nose-pressing for the ignorant
Mahāvākya 5

reconciliation.explanation: The Śāṇḍilya names two ways of ending mind — yoga and knowledge — suited to different people, and the Varāha's bird and ant paths both reach Brahman.
reconciliation.detail: Śāṇḍilya 1.41 (P3) and Varāha 4.34–42 (P4) treat yoga and knowledge as routes for different temperaments and stages; the Tejobindu keeps the limbs but reads them as knowledge.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yogaśikhā explicitly rejects 'knowledge alone'; the Muktikā explicitly excludes yoga as a means of kaivalya.

notes: Related registry dispute: dsp:works-knowledge-grace.

question: Is Īśvara to be admitted, and is devotion to him a means to liberation? (Yoga against nirīśvara Sāṃkhya)

sides.position: Īśvara is a special puruṣa, ever free, unsurpassed in knowledge, the teacher of the ancients, designated by Oṃ; devotion to him brings samādhi near.
arguments: The seed of omniscience admits degrees, so it has a limit where it is unsurpassed (YBh 1.25).
Two equal lords could not both have their contrary wishes fulfilled, so lordship without equal exists (YBh 1.24).
Won over by devotion, Īśvara favours the yogin by mere intention (YBh 1.23).

Vijñānabhikṣu: Sāṃkhya teaches liberation from knowledge of the self alone; Yoga shows knowledge of the Supreme Lord as the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51), and Sāṃkhya is contained in Yoga as rivers in the ocean (YV intro.).

sides.position: Liberation comes from discriminating knowledge of puruṣa and prakṛti; Īśvara is not established by any means of knowledge and is not needed to explain the working of prakṛti.
arguments: Prakṛti acts for the puruṣa's purpose unconsciously, as milk flows for the calf (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 57).
'Because Īśvara is not established' (Sāṃkhya Sūtra 1.92).
sides.note: Stated from memory in Sāṃkhya's own terms; U09 owns the Sāṃkhya texts.

historical_debates.name: The Sāṃkhya–Yoga contest reported by Bhīṣma
historical_debates.accounts: Mahābhārata 12 (Mokṣadharma; c. ch. 289 CE): the Yogins argue 'how can one without a Lord be liberated?', the Sāṃkhyas praise knowledge; both are declared valid. Recalled from memory, reference to be checked.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both views accepted as leading to the highest goal.

reconciliation.explanation: The Gītā (5.4–5) and the Mokṣadharma treat Sāṃkhya and Yoga as two approaches to one goal (P3), and Vijñānabhikṣu reads the Sāṃkhya denial of Īśvara as a provisional, concessive argument (P5).
reconciliation.detail: What is reconciled is the soteriological convergence (both end in discriminative knowledge and kaivalya); the ontological question whether a special puruṣa exists is not settled by P3.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nirīśvara Sāṃkhya authors argue on their own terms that Īśvara is unproven, not merely provisionally set aside; Vijñānabhikṣu's reading is a Yoga-Vedānta commentator's view.

notes: Narrower recorded debate within dsp:isvara (owned by U50).
